player.seasonOutlook: Chourio's rookie season is tough to appreciate until it's put into the proper context. He became only the 17th rookie in history to register a 20/20 season, with his .275 batting average ranking ninth amongst that group, and he finished 49th overall on our Player Rater and tied for 86th in fantasy points scored. Looking closer, Chourio began the season just 18 days past his 20th birthday, fresh off signing a record-setting contract for a player with no MLB experience, while also bearing a reputation for initial struggles when climbing competitive levels. He did stumble initially, with a .623 OPS through his first 67 games, but then he took off. Chourio's .309 batting average across his final 81 contests was ninth-best among qualifiers, and he scored the 11th-most fantasy points among hitters during that time span. The sky's the limit for this kid, who could very quickly establish himself as a perennial first-round fantasy pick in any format.

After a sluggish start to his Mets career, Lindor has recaptured his form as one of baseball's best all-around players. He has managed at least 31 home runs, 91 RBI, 29 stolen bases and 107 runs scored in both of the last two seasons, and showed decidedly improved raw power metrics. In fact, Lindor's strong finish to 2024 -- he hit .306/.368/.575 with 16 homers after the All-Star break -- hints at a possibly larger step forward in 2025. As the Mets made a big splash in free agency -- some guy named Soto -- Lindor's surging metrics come at an opportune time, as the team's offense should enjoy a noticeable boost from top to bottom. Lindor is a top-25 overall pick who, with some good fortune, could deliver first-round fantasy production.

Turner was limited to 121 games last season as a left hamstring strain cost him a bit over six weeks in May and June. He continues to be productive on the wrong side of 30, though anyone so reliant on his legs takes on a little more risk with each season. Turner's sprint speed registered in the 96th percentile in 2024, so the league's smoothest slider still has wheels. Turner's quality of contact is around league average, so he needs speed to continue to be among the league leaders in infield hits. Last season, Turner stole 10 bases in 33 games before getting hurt, but then he swiped just four bags in the subsequent 63 contests after returning before adding five more over his final 25 games, with the lull in the middle was likely due to protecting his hamstring. Turner is no longer among the elite shortstops, but he heads up the next tier.

In almost any other year, Merrill's 2024 breakthrough would have secured him a Rookie of the Year Award. He became only the fifth rookie in history with at least a .290 batting average, 20 HR, 90 RBI and 15  SB. The previous four all took home top rookie honors (Orlando Cepeda 1958, Nomar Garciaparra 1997, Carlos Beltran 1999, Ryan Braun 2007). Tuck that away if Merrill's value in your draft remotely softens, especially in light of his late-season skills improvement, as he hit .314/.349/.596 with 7% more fly balls after the All-Star break than before it. He no longer carries shortstop eligibility, but that doesn't make him any less attractive of an outfield pick in the early rounds. In keeper leagues, Merrill is a building block.

A popular preseason pick for 2024 AL Rookie of the Year honors, Langford instead struggled mightily in his first taste of the majors, batting just .227/.287/.300 with only seven extra-base hits across his first 40 games. As many a rookie has done before, however, he picked up the pace from there, culminating in June AL Rookie of the Month and September AL Player and Rookie of the Month honors. For the season as a whole, Langford's metrics were well above-average across the board, giving hope that the superstardom predicted for him at this point one year ago remains his future track. He should not be allowed to linger too deep into the middle rounds of any draft.

Rooker's arrival on the fantasy baseball scene has been quite unexpected. After changing teams three times during the course of 2022, he began 2023 as a platoon man only to burst forth with 30 homers. He followed it up with an even bigger breakthrough, finishing among the top eight in the majors with his 39 homers and a 16.6% Barrel rate in 2024. So where does Rooker, who signed a five-year, $60 million extension in January, go from here? The Athletics' move to Sacramento places them in a more hitter-friendly home environment for 2025, and the team's rekindled commitment to spending strengthened his prospects for a fantasy repeat. Even as a DH-only player initially, Rooker is well worth a mid-round pick.

Nola is only a one-time All-Star, with his lone All-Star appearance coming back in 2018. While he may not receive much attention nationally, Nola is one of the game's most dependable arms, having made at least 32 starts in each of the last six full MLB seasons. He shaved almost a run off his ERA in 2024 and fell just three strikeouts short of reaching 200 Ks for the sixth consecutive full season. His knuckle curve remains an excellent swing-and-miss pitch and his four-seamer was more effective last year, as opponents combined to bat just .168 against the offering. The right-hander can get bit by the long ball on occasion, and in fact Nola led the National League in homers allowed last season. That said, he still does so much well and won't turn 32 until June. Until further notice, Nola should be considered one of the best No. 2 starters in baseball.

Between the addition of a splitter and some good fortune on batted balls as well as in stranding runners, Miller took a huge step forward during his sophomore season. He finished among the top-50 overall players both on our Player Rater as well as in fantasy points scored, and even posted 10 quality starts, a 1.75 ERA and an 0.84 WHIP over his 13 second-half starts. Considering Miller's strand rate placed second, his BABIP sixth and his HR/FB percentage ninth during that latter stretch, regression should be expected as he enters year No. 3. His splitter, however, gives him a more legitimate out pitch, and his control is strong enough that he should cruise his way to a top-40 SP season even if his ratios take a step backwards.

Imanaga got off to a historic start with the Cubs last season, posting a 0.84 ERA across his first 53.2 innings, the lowest mark ever through a pitcher's first nine MLB starts. The lefty earned an All-Star selection in his first season stateside and finished third in the National League with 15 wins, while only George Kirby and Tarik Skubal ranked higher among qualified starters in terms of strikeout-to-walk ratio. Home runs were a problem on occasion -- Imanaga allowed multiple homers seven times -- and those concerns will follow him into 2025, as fantasy managers may hold their breath in tough matchups. The Cubs are working with him on that issue, and overall his stuff translated quite well as he made the jump from Nippon Professional Baseball at 30 years old. Expect some giveback, but Imanaga looks like a legitimate frontline starter, one probably best viewed as an SP2 for fantasy purposes.

Few pitchers have ever possessed the kind of control that Kirby has shown. His 3.1% walk rate, through three MLB seasons, is already the lowest among pitchers with at least as many starts as he has during the modern era. But don't conflate that for a pitcher who peppers the strike zone with so-so stuff. Kirby's 96.0 mph fastball, slider, sinker, splitter and knuckle curve gives him a sound, consistently elite repertoire that should make him an annual candidate for top-10 fantasy SP seasons. In order to take the next step and perhaps score big Cy Young votes, he'd probably need to reintroduce his whiff-generating splitter of 2023, but even without it he's the kind of pitcher around whom you'll want to build.

William Contreras finished last season on an island alone as the No. 1 fantasy catcher, but Diaz was right there in that second tier of earners just behind Cal Raleigh and Salvador Perez, at least in traditional leagues scoring batting average. Diaz finished fifth at the position in plate appearances with 619 and ranked eighth among all qualified hitters with a .299 average. It was an impressive showing after the Astros turned over the reins behind the plate, even if Diaz wasn't able to replicate the kind of power he showed as a rookie in 2023. In fact, Diaz hit seven fewer homers in 44 additional games. Nonetheless, Diaz established himself further and will be treated as a top catching option behind the younger Contreras entering 2025. Those in OBP leagues will likely want to bump Diaz down to account for a career walk rate of just 3.6 percent.

Iglesias and Atlanta has been a match made in heaven, as he's posted a 1.96 ERA and 0.92 WHIP in 151.1 innings spanning 152 appearances over the past two and a half seasons. He shaved his WHIP to just 0.74 last season and reached the 30-save threshold for the fifth time in his career. Iglesias lost a little bit off his strikeout rate and benefited from a .199 BABIP, but that's picking nits. All four of his pitches had BAAs under .180 and he went without allowing an earned run for about half the season from mid-June to mid-September. Now 35 years old, Iglesias will be pitching for a big payday next winter in the final year of his deal. There's always a chance he could be dealt if Atlanta falls out of contention, but the right-hander enters the year with a ton of job security in his current situation.

Fried finds himself pitching for a new organization after spending the last nine seasons in the Atlanta organization, as the Yankees gave Fried a sizable deal despite the time missed in 2023 with a forearm strain as well as the neuritis in his pitching elbow in the middle of the 2024 season. The left-hander's ability to limit homers will be tested at Yankee Stadium, but left-center field being forgiving to his particular approach -- at least on paper -- should help balance things out in his favor. Fried throws seven different pitch types to both righties and lefties which puts hitters into uncomfortable situations. His ability to keep hitters off balance is why he is elite at limiting hard contact and why his ERA has just once been above 3.25 in a full season of work. The only risk associated with Fried would be a recurrence of the forearm issue from 2023 as the skills are more than steady.

Gausman wasn't quite himself last year after a bout of shoulder fatigue in spring training interrupted his preparations for the start of the season. The right-hander's velocity was down a tick in 2024 -- several ticks early on -- and the strikeouts dipped along with it. His surface numbers improved over the final two months, but the strikeouts never really rebounded, as he was below a 20 percent K rate in both August and September. Just one year ago, Gausman was treated as a borderline ace following a late-career breakout built on the strength of his trademark splitter. The market has perhaps overcorrected heading into 2025, though the massive decline in whiffs and tough division leave performance question marks and provide reason to invest elsewhere. Now 34, Gausman has two years remaining on his deal with the Blue Jays.

Walker has been in the San Francisco system since being drafted out of Washington State in 2018. He made the slow climb up the organizational ladder as a reliever and finally made the big-league roster in 2023. This past season was the coming-out party, as Walker ended up as the primary closer for the Giants by the end of the season and was one of just two relievers to make at least 75 appearances and work at least 80 innings in 2024. While most pitchers have taken a step backward historically after such a season, Walker could pull a Brad Hand from 2016 and 2017 and repeat his success. Walker's delivery and stuff make it very tough for hitters to square him up, and with the closer job in hand, the right-hander is in great shape for 25-plus saves in 2025.

Stott now has three big-league seasons under his belt. He has the skills and athleticism to hit higher in the lineup for another team, but it will be for him to crack the top third of the Philadelphia order while Kyle Schwarber, Trea Turner and Bryce Harper are healthy. If stuck in the nine hole, his RBI chances will remain limited. Stott is one of just three second basemen to register double-digit homers and steals in each of the past three seasons, joining only Jose Altuve and Mookie Betts. Stott contributes across the board and some BABIP regression would help him recover some of the 35 points in batting average he lost from 2023 to 2024.

?The Martian? figures to take over starting left field duties for the Yankees in 2025 and, while his defense often came into question during a late-season audition last year, his Triple-A dominance in 2023-24 (.325/.391/.495 rates, 7 HR, 18 SB in 53 games) reflects his immense offensive potential. Dominguez is one of the more important hitters to watch during spring training, as more patience and more lift in his swing than he showed in his two cups of coffee with the Yankees could do him a world of good. He should be a good source of stolen bases at the very least, a back-of-the-roster mixed-league player at the median, and a breakthrough player with building-block dynasty potential at his best.

Rengifo was not in the Opening Day lineup for the Angels last season and ended up making three separate trips to the injured list, which kept him 80 games played. First he dealt with a viral infection that caused painful blisters on his feet, while wrist trouble shelved him on the other two occasions. Despite those issues, Rengifo swiped 24 bags in 31 attempts, showing an entirely new level with his speed after he had previously topped out at six steals in a season. He also hit an even .300 during his time on the field, up close to 40 points from 2023, though it's difficult to fully buy into either new element of his game given the sample size and Rengifo's performance history. That said, Rengifo has more pop than he showed last season, and while he is no longer quad-eligible like he was entering 2024, he still qualifies at third base and second base, providing valuable flexibility.

Pena now has three full major-league seasons under his belt. He has hit 20 homers in a season and he has also stolen 20 bases in a season, but the shortstop has been unable to accomplish both feats in the same campaign. Pena has the pull tendencies one would like to see from someone playing in Houston and hitting from the right side, but his high groundball rate limits his home-run power. Pena has improved his strikeout rate each season he has been in the majors, but he has not shown any willingness to accepts walks. Pena has also stolen double-digit bases each season, but his success rate has been below league average since the rule adjustments two seasons ago. His impatience puts him in the bottom half of the lineup which limits his overall upside, and it's a shame because Pena's numbers could be much better if he were setting the table ahead of the thunder in the lineup.

Neto broke out last season to the tune of 23 homers and 30 steals in 155 games for the Angels. Despite that, the fantasy world is treating the shortstop with some trepidation entering his age-24 season in 2025. Most pertinently, his availability for the start of the upcoming season is uncertain after he underwent right shoulder surgery in November. Neto was also caught stealing 10 times and managed just a .697 OPS against right-handed pitching. The concerns are valid, but Neto improved his OBP and SLG significantly in the second half and his playing time will be locked in once he completes his recovery from surgery. His batted-ball profile leaves a lot to be desired, but this kind of power-speed combo is tough to find outside of the early rounds, even if it is largely volume driven.

What toe problem? Judge, who missed 42 games after tearing a ligament in his right big toe crashing into an outfield wall in June 2023, entered 2024 facing legitimate questions about future maintenance of the ailment. Instead, he delivered a season for the ages: MLB-leading numbers in home runs, RBIs, walks (133), OBP (.458), slugging (.701), OPS (1.159), OPS-plus (223) and Wins Above Replacement (10.8). Oh, yes, and a career-high 158 games played. Judge's contact-quality metrics are off the charts -- he has paced the majors in expected wOBA, Barrel and hard-hit rates among hitters with at least as many plate appearances as his in each of the past three seasons -- and he's among the game's most selective hitters, even if his game has lots of swing-and-miss. There aren't many more well-rounded players to select with a first-round fantasy draft pick.

A shin contusion that later revealed a small fracture, costing the right fielder 79 games, might be the one thing holding Tucker back from entering 2025 as one of fantasy baseball's most prominent superstars. At the time of the injury, caused by his fouling a pitch off his shin, he was on pace for a 50/27 season and 112 runs scored, continuing his pattern as one of baseball's most reliable five-category rotisserie performers. Tucker returned in September with a flourish, batting .365 with four homers across 18 games, giving confidence that he should resume in 2025 where he left off in his walk year with his new team, the Cubs. In fact, he might have room to grow, considering 2024 saw him set new personal bests with his 16.5% walk, 17.5% chase, 41.3% fly ball and 12.9% Barrel rates.

Although his six-year MLB career hasn't yet reached the stratospheric levels that his Hall of Fame father's did, Junior has had some impressive exploits in his own right. Guerrero's 2024 saw him set personal bests in batting average, doubles, contact and whiff rates. It was his third 30-HR campaign and the fourth year in a row with at least 94 RBI. His contact-quality metrics rate among the best in the game, as his Statcast expected batting average across the past four seasons (.303) is fifth-best (minimum 1,200 plate appearances). Plus, he has played in all but 12 Blue Jays games during that time. The primary thing holding Guerrero back from an early first-round valuation is his ground ball-oriented swing. If he could once again show the kind of lift he did during his 48-HR 2021, he'd contend for an MVP award.

Henderson followed up his unanimous 2023 Rookie of the Year season with a 2024 that saw him hit 26 home runs through the Orioles' first 80 games, second-most in the majors (Aaron Judge, 30), and finish fourth in AL MVP balloting. While Henderson cooled somewhat in the power department during the season's second half -- nine home runs and .174 ISO in his final 64 contests -- his cumulative numbers nevertheless cemented him as one of the game's premier shortstops, both for real life and fantasy. He's a centerpiece of one of the game's best up-and-coming offenses and a genuine, annual 35/20 threat. He is a building-block piece in both points-based and dynasty leagues.

While not a lock, Machado might very well be headed to Cooperstown one day, and he continued to produce at a high level in 2024. The third baseman smacked 29 homers and finished third in the National League with 105 RBI, marking the third time he's cleared the century mark in the last four seasons. Machado's OBP has dipped in recent years as his patience has waned, but he continues to hit the ball hard and remains a model of good health, clearing 600 plate appearances in each of the last nine full MLB seasons. He endured a rough month of May and grounded into 25 double plays last year, most in the majors, which speaks to his reduced mobility at 32 years old. Perhaps he will be a bit more susceptible to streakiness moving forward, but for now, Machado can still be a viewed as a foundational piece of any fantasy offense.

Senga's sophomore season in MLB never really got off the ground, as a shoulder strain put him on the shelf to begin the campaign and he strained his calf in his very first start back in July, costing him the rest of the regular season. He returned to make three appearances in the postseason, including a surprise start in Game 1 of the NLCS, pitching a total of five innings. That should have set the right-hander up for a relatively normal offseason, though workload expectations will be difficult to pin down after the lost year. He was able to overcome a high walk rate in his first season with the Mets after the making the jump from Japan. If healthy in 2025, Senga could continue to outperform the estimators thanks to the quality of his repertoire and the league's general discombobulation with his ghost forkball.

After Devin Williams was lost for four months due to back issues and neither Abner Uribe nor Joel Payamps proved up to the role, Megill swooped in and converted 20-of-22 save chances, his 99-mph fastball and knuckle curve also making him a strong source of strikeouts. With Williams now in New York, Megill figures to get the first crack at the Brewers' closer job to begin 2025, from which he has the skills to be a solid second-tier fantasy option. His so-so walk rate and penchant for fly balls make him slightly riskier than the position's top-tier names, but he's well worth a selection in the middle rounds.

The primary return for the Rays in the Tyler Glasnow trade, Pepiot slotted directly into the team's rotation with a productive, top-60 SP fantasy season. Most notably, he rebounded from multiple IL stints due to fluky circumstances (a leg injury after being struck by a liner, a bug bite that led to a knee infection) to set professional bests in starts and innings pitched as well as a 2.95 ERA and 25.7% strikeout rate across his final nine starts. It sets Pepiot up for another similarly, if not a couple of tiers better, productive 2025. Now, the Rays' move to George M. Steinbrenner Field will set him back from a park factor perspective and the team's tendency to mix and match on the pitching side might prevent a big innings bump. Even so, he's a solid fourth or fifth mixed-league starter.

A three-homer game during the second full week of the season set the tone for Langeliers' 2024 campaign, as he finished second on the team to Brent Rooker in both home runs and RBI with 29 and 80, respectively. Langeliers cut a couple points off his strikeout rate which helped lift his batting average from .205 to a slightly more palatable .224. Slugging will have to carry Langeliers' offensive game since he has a strikeout rate of nearly 30 percent for his career, and the Athletics' move to a Pacific Coast League park in West Sacramento should help in that regard in 2025. Even with the low average and limited time at DH to boost his stats, Langeliers will likely be drafted as a top-10 catcher in many leagues.

Ward established new career highs in plate appearances (663), hits (144) and home runs (25) last season, leading the Angels in all three categories. He still has not been able to replicate the full extent of his success from 2022 when he slashed .281/.360/.473 over 564 plate appearances, but Ward's 2024 season represented a bright spot for the organization as well as an impressive personal rebound. Remember, his 2023 campaign was cut short when he suffered multiple facial fractures on a hit-by-pitch and there are often mental hurdles that accompany such an injury. Ward's strikeout rate ticked up to close to 25 percent last season, but he was still an above-average offensive contributor, and as he enters his age-31 season, he appears set to continue anchoring the heart of the order for Anaheim.

While many might regard Torres' career thus far as a disappointment, he has nevertheless carved out a plenty productive role for himself. Over his seven MLB seasons, his 138 home runs rank third-most among second basemen and he's one of only four at the position with at least 100 homers and 50 steals. Torres did benefit from the hitter-friendly home environment of Yankee Stadium, as well as the often potent Yankees lineup, so some regression is to be expected now that he's a member of the Tigers. Still, Torres seems to have settled in as an annual 25-HR, 10-SB, .265-hitting type with top-10 positional fantasy value. Plus, he did finish an underwhelming 2024 on a high note (.297/.369/.453, 7 HR over his final 45 games, playoffs included). Expect similar value from him in 2025.

Martinez began the season with Triple-A Reno, but after punching out 14 hitters in 6.2 innings, he was called up in mid-April. Early on, he worked in low-leverage scenarios, notching his first hold June 4. Martinez then serves as a setup man until August when he took over as the primary closer for Arizona. He converted eight of nine chances over the final two months and Martinez has stuff to continue closing as he averages triple digits on his four-seam fastball and sinker, though can struggle to locate on occasion. His WHIP will be high with the walks, so saves will come with ratio baggage. Just 23 years old, Martinez can certainly learn to throw more strikes. He'll enter the season as the favorite for saves in the desert, though A.J. Puk looms if Martinez's control issues yield too many blown saves.

Estrada was a fantasy sleeper for a couple of years, but after he punched out 13 hitters in a row last May, everyone's eyes were wide open. He proceeded to post an impressive campaign, helping the Padres make the postseason. Once the Cubs' closer of the future, the 26-year-old righty could be in line to fulfill that destiny with the Padres, though he'll have to wait with Robert Suarez slated for ninth-inning duties and Jason Adam next in line as the primary setup man. Still, Estrada will garner high-leverage work and has a chance to join the 100-strikeout club while racking up holds.

Although a lat strain cost him more than three months of time, Schmidt's 2024 reflected important signs of growth. He boosted his innings-per-start average by 0.38 and his K rate by nearly 5%. He also lowered his wOBA against lefties by nearly 70 points compared to 2023, and he was allowed to throw 100-plus pitches five times, his first such starts as a major leaguer. Schmidt still needs to add stamina in order to reach the upper tier of fantasy starters, but his incremental gains year over year bode well for his taking another step in 2025. Consider him in the mid-to-late rounds in mixed leagues deeper than ESPN's standard.

Vaughn is one of just 12 first-base-eligible players to have logged at least 550 plate appearances in each of the past three seasons. There is value in volume, but how much actual production Vaughn will bring to the table is debatable with all the uncertainty surrounding the Chicago roster. There have been rumors of them dealing Luis Robert, which could affect Vaughn's already limited RBI chances. Vaughn has not embraced the heavy pull tendencies that most corner sluggers do which has put a cap on any projected home-run total despite his ability to make better-than-average contact. Vaughn is projected to hit cleanup for the White Sox and there is little reason to think he won't turn in similar counting stats since his profile has been remarkably stable for a young hitter to date. He simply lacks the power profile that most chase at the first base position.

After 13 starts spanning 58 innings, Arrighetti registered a 6.36 ERA and 1.74 WHIP. His 23.8% strikeout rate was encouraging, but his 12.8% walk rate was concerning. However, something clicked at that point, and Arrighetti posted a 3.31 ERA and 1.18 WHIP over his final 87 frames. He threw more changeups in lieu of fastballs later in the season, along with improving control. Maintaining the drop will be a tall order, but Arrighetti's strikeout rate and the Astros' penchant for finding what works warrants drafting Arrighetti as a matchup play that could develop into more.

Fresh off his unanimous 2023 NL Rookie of the Year campaign -- one that saw him become the first rookie in baseball history with at least 25 home runs and 50 stolen bases -- Carroll spent the first half of 2024 making a compelling case for fantasy bust of the year. A near-universal first round pick, he entered the All-Star break batting just .213 with five home runs, three of which came in the eight days leading into it, as he struggled throughout to adapt to swing changes he had implemented the prior winter. Carroll finally got it together during the second half, hitting .259/.351/.568 with 17 homers and 17 steals in 64 games, a welcome sign that the rotisserie superstar of old had returned. Just 24, Carroll would surely benefit from better luck on balls in play, but all signs have him returning to near top-10 form in 2025. It's just a year too late for those who drafted him that way last spring.

Tatis was limited to 102 games last season due to a stress reaction in his right femur. His production was an improvement over a down 2023 season, but it fell short of the lofty standards established over the first three years of his career. The main difference was a drop in power fueled by a slightly lower average exit velocity on flyballs, though his barrel rate was still 92nd percentile. Tatis ran less last season with only 11 steals in 14 tries, though it is encouraging that he was 3-for-3 in September after returning from the leg injury. After he stole a total of 54 bases on 62 attempts over his two seasons prior to last, it's reasonable to expect more running this season, putting the 26-year-old in the first-round discussion.

Crochet didn't merely break out in his first season back in a pitching rotation since his Tennessee days -- his 2024 performance was historic. He became the first pitcher in the modern era to strike out at least 140 batters with 20 walks or fewer through his first 18 career starts, and seven consecutive strikeouts to begin his Sept. 1 start tied an AL record. Despite the White Sox's concerns about his workload, which increased over the course of the summer, Crochet maintained elite underlying skills, even if his 5.12 second-half ERA belied his talent. The Red Sox acquired him with the hopes he can further blossom into their staff ace. Considering his arrow pointed nowhere but up for the entirety of 2024, there's reason to believe he will. Crochet is a building-block pitcher for fantasy purposes.

Devers is one of the game's more underappreciated raw power sources, probably in large part because he has never even placed among the top 10 in MVP balloting across eight MLB seasons. Nevertheless, he's the only hitter who can claim at least 30 doubles, 25 homers and a .500 slugging percentage in each of the past four seasons, during which time his Statcast average exit velocities and hard-hit rates have all rated in at least the 92nd percentile. Remarkably, Devers can claim that despite having been hampered by shoulder issues that cost him 11 of Boston's final 31 games and caused him to hit just .177 with one extra-base hit (a double) in the other 19. With a clean bill of health during spring training, he could be primed for a return to the 35-HR plateau. Draft him accordingly.

Acuna's seven-year MLB career has been quite the rollercoaster ride. He has won NL Rookie of the Year (2018) and MVP Awards (2023). He's had a 41/37 campaign (2019) and the majors' first-ever 40/70 season (2023) on his résumé, yet has also dealt with three separate ACL injuries (among other ailments) including surgeries on both of his knees (the right in 2021, the left in 2024). Fantasy managers should heed Acuna's performance initially returning from surgery the last time, as he missed the first three weeks of 2022 while recovering, then finished 65th on the Player Rater and tied for 175th in fantasy points scored. A sluggish start could be his downside -- tuck that away as a strategic nugget to perhaps instead trade for him in-season -- but his upside remains that of a five-category rotisserie superstar. If reports on his health during spring training look good, he shouldn't slide much further than the first couple of rounds of rotisserie drafts, nor far outside the top-25 overall in points leagues.

DeGrom has managed to put up just 197.1 innings over the past four seasons due to his body constantly failing him, which is a shame considering he's one of the best pitchers of this generation. The right-hander last worked a full season in 2019 when he pitched his third consecutive season of 200-plus innings while winning his second consecutive Cy Young Award. He made it back for three starts at the end of 2024 and essentially picked up where he left off with 14 strikeouts and one walk over those outings. This remains the ultimate risk/reward pick because at least Tyler Glasnow is good for 100-plus innings in a season around his injuries while deGrom has barely worked 100 innings over the previous three seasons combined. Even 100 innings of deGrom brilliance would be more valuable to a roster than 150 innings of another arm, but expecting that sort of workload might be optimistic.

Woodruff looked like a rising star for Milwaukee not long ago, earning All-Star selections in 2019 and 2021. However, he has missed the better part of two seasons due to injury, including all of 2024, after undergoing surgery in October of 2023 to repair the anterior capsule in his right shoulder. While the Brewers will not commit to Woodruff being ready for Opening Day 2025, he was said to be in a good spot and throwing multiple bullpen sessions per week in January. Entering his age-32 season, Woodruff is a wild card for both the Brewers and fantasy managers. The innings floor is zilch and the workload ceiling is capped, but Woodruff's excellent track record of performance (career 3.10 ERA, 1.05 WHIP) will likely tempt some to roll the dice outside the top 200 picks or so overall.

Hoffman broke through in a big way in 2023 while pitching in middle relief for the Phillies. Last season, he upped the ante even further by slashing another 3% off his walk rate. Between that and his sharing of the closer duties with Jose Alvarado, Carlos Estevez and Matt Strahm, Hoffman managed a top-20 season, both in rotisserie and points-based scoring. Now with the Blue Jays, Hoffman should take over full-time closer duties, a role from which he could take yet another step forward into the upper tier at his position. Draft him accordingly.

Even though Bibee's ERA in 2024 was half a run higher than his rookie season, he improved his strikeout and walk rates to the point his 20.1% K-BB% mark was the 13th best among qualified pitchers. His home run rate ticked up, but it was still below the league average. Bibee's four-seam fastball registered a -8.5 pitch value after landing at 6.5 in his rookie season. However, he generated more swinging strikes and threw it in the zone more often last season. Last year's Hard-Hit and Barrel Rates against were lower than his rookie season, but the BABIP on his four-seamer was higher, driving down the pitch value. Consider the oddity as something to monitor but not detract from his status as one of the top young starters in the game.

Chapman has not saved 15 games in a season since 2021, largely because of his propensity for walking batters, which is is too problematic for full-time closing duties. Yes, Chapman strikes out a high volume of hitters to offset his walks, but his walk rate has been at or above 15 percent each of the past four seasons. Walking a tight-rope in Pittsburgh is one thing; doing it in Fenway for half the season as well the other parks of the AL East is another. Boston also has other options such as Justin Slaten and the recovering Liam Hendriks for the ninth inning. Chapman's fastball velocity is still among the best in the league and homers are not as frequent as one might think. If Chapman could somehow get his walk rate back to a single-digit mark, he could once again be a high-end closer. However, that seems unlikely at 37 years old considering the fact Chapman has but once had a single-digit walk rate over the last eight seasons.

Pivetta has had his moments of fantasy greatness over the years, best exemplified on a cumulative basis by his having the 13th-most strikeouts across the past four seasons. Still, his hot spells have unfortunately been too few and too far between. Injuries, occasional wildness and an extreme fly-ball rate have been the obstacles standing in his path towards something more, though he did finish 2024 with a 3.92 ERA and a 29.7% strikeout rate across his final 14 starts. That gives some hope for a step forward. Pivetta did linger on the free-agent market deep into the winter, but so long as he lands a committed rotation spot somewhere, he'll be worth a mid-round pick with greater appeal in points league scoring.

The Cardinals announced in November that Contreras will be a full-time first baseman and designated hitter moving forward. It brings to an end a rather strange saga in which the team soured on his catching abilities shortly after signing him, moving him out from behind the plate for a stretch previously in 2023. Contreras fractured his forearm on a catcher's interference in May of last year when he was struck by a J.D. Martinez swing, and he broke a finger on a HBP later in the season. He still managed 15 home runs in just 84 games, and Contreras has been above league average at the plate in every single season of his career. Now 34 and overshadowed by his younger brother, Contreras will potentially get lost in the shuffle at first base when he loses catcher eligibility in 2026, but he should still be treated as a premium option at the catcher position for 2025.

A prospect's growth isn't always linear and a veteran's decline isn't always gradual. Case in point: Springer. There is a chance Springer enjoys a renaissance season in 2025, but his quality of contact metrics are quickly heading in the wrong direction and they usually don't reverse at 35 years old. Springer's hard-hit rate and average exit velocity were career lows last season. In addition, his groundball rate has increased each of the last three seasons, sapping power. Once a top-of-the-order mainstay, Springer is now best suited for the lower half of the lineup. Solid plate skills keep Springer fantasy relevant, but there is arguably more downside than upside at this stage.

Pressed into rotational duty with the Cardinals late last May, Pallante registered a 3.56 ERA and seven quality starts across 20 tries the rest of the way, his extreme ground ball repertoire making him a high-floor (albeit low-ceiling) fantasy starter. He'll return in the same role for the 2025 squad, where he'd probably need to improve his control in order to take a noticeable step forward. Pallante is the type of pitcher better used for streaming/matchups purposes in mixed leagues than trusted every time out, although he should be on NL-only managers' radar.

Ohtani has scripted quite the résumé already over his seven MLB seasons: Rookie of the Year (2018), MVP honors (2021), first player in history to hit 30-plus homers while also striking out 200-plus batters (2022), back-to-back MVPs (2023-24) and, most recently, becoming the charter member of baseball's 50/50 club (2024). While further history book rewrites might seem logically unattainable for the now-30-year-old, it's still within the realm of possibility that he'll score a career-high total fantasy points in 2025 and/or set a personal best in Wins Above Replacement. As both a hitter and pitcher from 2021-23 -- his expected role once again in 2025 -- Ohtani averaged 214 fantasy points more than the league's next-best player annually, an advantage that can be readily exploited in ESPN's standard game with its daily transaction format. Ohtani's fantasy utility hinges heavily upon how your league handles him, but a universal, No. 1 overall case is a relatively easy one.

Witt followed up his sizzling, 2023 second-half breakthrough with a 2024 that might have garnered him an MVP award (not to mention top placement on our fantasy leaderboards), if not for Shohei Ohtani and Aaron Judge. Witt became the first player to manage multiple 30/30 seasons before his 25th birthday, and the 11th shortstop of any age with a 30/30 campaign. He led the majors in batting average, and was one of only six players with at least 100 runs scored and 100 RBI. Witt is one of the game's few true five-category rotisserie superstars, his combination of solid contact and extra-base ability affording him the chance to challenge for the fantasy points leaderboard. Plus, he's still only 24 years old. If there's a nit to pick, it's that he attempted only 15 steals across his most recent 94 games (playoffs included), which could be as much small sample size noise as it might signal his seeing more red lights on the bases as his bat becomes more critical to the Royals' competitive chances.

The Mets have given Soto's fantasy managers 765 million reasons to trust in his elite talent. He's one of six players in history to register a .400 OBP in each of his first seven seasons, and one of three from that group (Ted Williams, Frank Thomas) to also manage at least a 140 OPS-plus in each year. Soto's 201 career home runs before turning 26 are also tied for sixth-most in history, and he's the only player to register a top-15 fantasy point total among hitters in each of the past six seasons. He is the epitome of the high-floor, safe return on investment first-round pick, even if his profit potential is greater in leagues that reward his patience. Nevertheless, Soto could be headed for a prime-years uptick, playing the 2025 season at the age of 26.

Ray's rehab from May 2023 Tommy John surgery extended into late July, and from there, he managed to make just seven starts before being shut down in late August with a strained hamstring. Ray threw 30.2 innings with 43 punchouts and 15 walks, along with six homers. His velocity returned to 2021 levels and his path looks typical for a pitcher recovering from TJS -- the strikeouts come back first, and then command and control. Ray struggles with home runs, making it all the more important that he limit the free passes. His home venue is ideal for streaming, but it may be best to wait and gauge his health and command in the spring before investing.

Sale's Comeback Player of the Year campaign earned him his first career Cy Young Award in 2024, fueled by what were his best single-year strikeout, whiff and hard-hit rates allowed as well as his best average fastball velocity since before his March 2020 Tommy John surgery. Best yet, he only seemed to improve as the season progressed, posting a 1.88 ERA and a 33.2% strikeout rate across his final 16 starts, signaling his ability to maintain an elite level of performance despite his 35 years of age. Back issues prematurely ended Sale's campaign. That's an injury which bears watching throughout spring training, but if he's in the clear on that front, he's plenty capable of delivering top-10 fantasy SP numbers again.

Only a left ankle sprain which cost him three weeks in late August/early September stood in Marte's way towards cementing his status as one of fantasy baseball's most productive hitters, but perhaps that missed time (and how it influences the perception of his worth) will merely serve to keep him affordable come draft day. He set personal bests with his 36 home runs and 95 RBI, fully supported by huge spikes in contact quality. His hard-hit rate was 14% greater than his career number in the category and he made huge strides defensively at second base. For you daily-transactions folks, bear in mind that his .414 wOBA against left-handed pitchers over the past five seasons is third-best in baseball (minimum 150 plate appearances). Consider taking Marte, a top-25 performer in both fantasy points and on our Player Rater last year, in the opening rounds of any draft.

Buxton exclusively worked at designated hitter throughout 2023 in an attempt to keep him healthy, but he played in just 85 contests before returning to center field for the Twins last season. His return to the outfield was overall a success as his 102 games played represented his largest workload since 2017, but he still battled injuries and has reached 400 plate appearances in a season just once in his big-league career. Buxton took a major step backward at the plate in 2023, but he rebounded last year with 18 home runs and a .279/.335/.524 slash line, with the resurgence being supported by a 48.1 percent hard-hit rate. The 31-year-old has played in just over 57 percent of Minnesota's games across the past three seasons, so 90-100 games is a reasonable estimate for him in 2025. Fantasy managers will obviously be hoping for more than that, especially coming off a clean offseason, but expectations should still be tempered given his lengthy injury history.

Ragans' follow-up to his astonishing, late-2023 breakthrough went about as well as could possibly have been expected. He maintained almost every statistical gain across his by-far professional bests of 32 starts and 186 1/3 IP, with the only knock on his skills being his losing a tick on his average fastball velocity. Throwing 95.4 mph, however, makes him no slouch in terms of raw stuff, and pitching half of his games in one of the most pitcher-friendly environments helps bolster his case to be a true staff ace. Ragans should be drafted among the top 10 at his position, regardless of format.

Whereas most catchers wear down rather quickly due the rigors of the position, Perez is still running strong at nearly 35 years old. He exceeded 100 RBI last season for the second time in his career and surged past 20 homers once again en route to his fifth Silver Slugger Award. Perez is the active leader in games played at catcher and 58th on the all-time list. The Royals have made a concerted effort to limit Perez's time behind the plate in recent years, giving him more time at first base and DH, which makes all the sense in the world given the mileage on Perez's knees and with Freddy Fermin proving plenty capable of helping with the workload. Perez is firmly in the old-and-boring category, but his track record of power production from the catcher spot should keep his services in high demand in fantasy baseball.

An oblique strain put Muncy on the shelf in May and eventually forced a move to the 60-day injured list since he was slow to progress. He finally made it back in August and was a regular in the lineup throughout the Dodgers' run to the World Series, doing typical Muncy things with a .163 average but also three homers and 15 walks in the postseason. At 34 years old, Muncy is well established as a low-average, high-OBP slugger from the left side. Given the depth in Los Angeles and his splits in recent years, it seems likely that he will remain limited to a platoon, starting primarily against right-handed pitching. That in theory limits his upside, but Muncy's immense power and the lineup around him make him a potential option at third base or corner infield once the everyday players are off the board.

Here's one of the most disappointing players of 2024, as his ADP in ESPN leagues was 18th overall, but he finished 55th on the Player Rater and tied for 170th in fantasy points. Rodriguez, only 24, has plenty of time to straighten things out.  Besides, his season wasn't a complete catastrophe, as he joined Mike Trout and Bobby Witt Jr. as the only three players in history to manage 20/20 numbers in each of their first three full MLB seasons. He also maintained strong underlying metrics in terms of his contact quality and raw speed, and he managed .295/.345/.486 rates, nine home runs and six stolen bases across his final 43 games after returning from a mid-year ankle injury. Rodriguez remains one of the game's most talented young players, albeit one who has shown a tendency for slow starts and is more of a rotisserie than points-based prospective star. He remains a strong early-round pick, especially in roto.

After teasing a late-career power surge in 2023, Diaz reverted to his previous power levels last season. Overall, Diaz continues to sport elite quality of contact metrics, but since he hits grounders more than half of the time, he is unable to take full advantage. Not only did Diaz's power drop, but his batting average with runners in scoring position fell 90 points, limiting his RBI. After carrying a double-digit walk rate over the previous five seasons, Diaz's patience waned last season, leaving him with the second-lowest OBP of his career. Diaz is best suited for points leagues, where his high doubles total can help mitigate fewer homers. Look for a rebound, but 2023 will likely go down as Diaz's career year.

Adam has been on a three-year tear since being plucked by the Rays off the free-agent wire when the Cubs didn't see what they had. He has shown the ability to step in for saves when needed as well as contribute to all five pitching categories. Adam's success comes from his ability to throw four different pitch types to both righties and lefties, and he will use any of his pitches at any time. This past season saw him improve his slider which was downright unhittable. Adam's .162 batting average against over the past three seasons leads all relievers with at least 150 innings pitched over that span, and he is 10 points lower than any other pitcher on that list. Robert Suarez is still the favorite for saves in San Diego, but Adam has value as a late-inning weapon and his value skyrockets should anything happen with Suarez.

Weaver's first season exclusively working out of the bullpen went swimmingly as he tied for third among relievers with 103 strikeouts in 2024. He added velocity to his fastball and cutter and used them more while reducing the usage of his slider and knuckle-curve. Weaver spent most of the season in a setup capacity, often throwing more than one inning before taking over as the Yankees closer down the stretch and into the playoffs, and he finished the campaign with four saves and 23 holds. Even so, the Yankees traded for Devin Williams, pushing Weaver back to garnering holds, though he's still likely to pick up the odd save, along with supporting ratios and strikeouts.

Kerkering's status as the Phillies' presumed closer of the future suffered a winter setback with the signing of Jordan Romano, but considering Romano's injuries in 2024, there might soon be ninth-inning opportunities for the youngster. Thanks to his trio of potentially elite offerings, Kerkering posted the sixth-best qualified ERA before the All-Star break (1.30) -- almost fully supported by his FIP (1.72) -- before taking a bit of a step back during the season's second half. Nevertheless, it exemplified his upside, and with Jeff Hoffman and Carlos Estevez no longer on the roster, it should lead to more high-leverage opportunities. Consider Kerkering to be one of the better breakout bets at his position.

Alcantara, the Cy Young Award winner in the National League in 2022, missed all of last season after undergoing Tommy John surgery in October of 2023. He advanced from regular side sessions to throwing live batting practice last September and will be nearly 18 months removed from the procedure by the time Opening Day rolls around. The Marlins have not publicly disclosed an innings target for Alcantara in 2025, but somewhere around 150 frames likes a good starting point, with room for more if his arm holds up. The injury concerns are not going away anytime soon with a pitcher that throws so hard, but if he proves healthy after the long layoff, Alcantara could prove to be a bargain for fantasy managers at his average draft position. Expect the acquisition cost to rise considerably if Alcantara is pumping gas and looking healthy in spring training.

After teasing fantasy managers for years with encouraging underlying metrics but so-so results, a tweak to his mechanics in late July finally spawned a breakthrough for Manaea. By lowering his arm angle, he added three full percentage points to his whiff rate and 6% to his ground-ball percentage across his final 12 regular-season starts, during which he had three double-digit strikeout games, a 3.09 ERA, a 28.4% K rate and the second-most fantasy points among pitchers (202). Whether Manaea can maintain those gains is a fair question as he had never before 2024 posted a full-season ERA lower than 3.50, but there's certainly top-40 SP potential here with the tweaks taken into account. He's worth a quick spring re-examination before investing at that price point, but his arrow is pointing upward.

After Brett Baty struggled and was returned to Triple-A, Vientos flourished as the Mets' regular third baseman across the season's final four months. He posted upper-tier raw power metrics while slashing more than 8% off his ground-ball rate, and his 24 homers from June 1 forward ranked fourth-best among third basemen and 12th-best in the majors. Still, Vientos' contact left a lot to be desired, as his 31.2% strikeout rate was seventh-worst over that same time span, which puts him at risk of lengthy cold spells and a low cumulative batting average. He's a legitimate power source with more rotisserie than points-based appeal, but be forewarned that he could be due for some regression in 2025.

Wacha has pitched for four different teams over the past four years, but he has found a home in Kansas City after his best season since 2015 which earned him a new three-year contract. Indeed, Wacha's numbers are impressive for a pitcher who does not exactly blow hitters away. The right-hander throws the kitchen sink at righties and lefties, serving up six different offerings to be exact, led by his great changeup. The addition of a slider in 2024 gave him two different shapes to his breaking ball to go along with the changeup and three fastball variations. What a pitcher lacks in velocity they have to make up for in pitch execution and craftiness, and Wacha is quite adept at both these days. He's no ace, but Wacha can help stabilize real and fantasy rotations.

A paragon of fantasy baseball excellence across the past nine seasons, Betts has hit .294 while averaging 30 home runs, 88 RBI, 19 stolen bases, 113 runs scored and 503 fantasy points per 162 team games over that time. His cumulative numbers in those categories rank ninth (minimum 2,000 plate appearances), seventh, ninth, ninth, first and second overall. Additionally, he entered both 2024 (OF/2B) and 2025 (OF/SS) with dual-positional eligibility and added additional eligibility in-season in 2023 (2B, SS) and 2024 (SS). Even at 32 years old, Betts appears primed for another year of steady, first round-caliber production, in large part due to his elite plate discipline and positioning atop the productive Dodgers lineup, one of the most fantasy-friendly roles in the league.

A model of consistency for more than a decade, Freeman has scored 400-plus fantasy points in eight of his 14 full MLB seasons, matching Mike Trout for the most by any player during that time span, while finishing among the top-25 overall on the Player Rater in five of the past seven years. Freeman's combination of polished approach at the plate and elite quality of contact makes him one of the highest-floor players in fantasy baseball, even as his age-35 season dawns. Sure, his so-so second half -- his .790 OPS after the All-Star break was his worst in any half-season since 2015's second half -- beckons questions about the aging curve, and the ankle injury that bothered him late in the year (and in the postseason) which required December surgery warrants a spring check-in. That said, Freeman is otherwise a rock-solid, foundational piece to select in your draft's opening rounds.

Injuries once again hampered Seager, who has now spent time on the IL in five of his past seven seasons, resulting in a combined 333 regular-season games missed over that stretch. A hip issue cut his 2024 short in early September, and hernia surgeries bookended his season (one in January, one in September). Nevertheless, Seager remained healthy enough to hit 30-plus homers for the third consecutive season and, at the time he got hurt, he had the sixth-most fantasy points among shortstops and 25th-most of all hitters. His underlying metrics, too, were as good as they have been at any point during the past five seasons, signaling that he's still every bit the early-round pick.

It's not often you'll see a catcher deliver the kind of breakthrough 2023 season that Contreras had and then following it up with an even more productive campaign. The No. 1 catcher from that year's Player Rater, and second-best in fantasy points, the Brewers backstop not only led his position in both scoring formats in 2024, but finished 28th in fantasy points and 44th on the Player Rater overall. Maintaining the contact and plate-discipline gains he exhibited two years ago was key to this transformation, and Contreras' jump into the 91st percentile in hard-hit rate last season reflects his status as one of the position's best power sources. He mashes left-handed pitchers -- FYI daily leaguers -- and should be the first catcher off the board in all fantasy formats.

The centerpiece of the 2023-24 offseason's Juan Soto trade, King proved every bit as capable a starting pitcher across 30 starts for the Padres last season as he was over an eight-start stint for the Yankees to conclude 2023. In fact, King was one of only four pitchers to strike out at least 200 batters with a sub-3.00 ERA, joining both Cy Young Award winners (Chris Sale, Tarik Skubal) and Zack Wheeler. He only strengthened his underlying numbers over the season's second half, getting a whiff nearly one-third of the time hitters swung at any of his pitches. It sets up the right-hander well for a similarly productive 2025, albeit with some risk of ERA regression, as his Statcast xERA should be nearly three-quarters of a run higher. Still, that's a top-20 capable fantasy starter regardless of format.

Castillo's season ended in early September as a result of a hamstring strain, but he's expected to be 100 percent in the spring. Previously more of an groundball pitcher in Great American Ball Park, he has adjusted to T-Mobile Park, inducing more flyballs. Even in the bigger yard, Castillo's homers have increased, though the corresponding drop in BABIP has lowered his WHIP, so he is no longer a detriment in that category. After two seasons with a strikeout rate over 27 percent, Castillo slid to 24.3 percent last season, coinciding with a drop in swinging-strike rate. His once vaunted changeup lost some of its effectiveness, likely due to his four-seam fastball dropping a couple of ticks. He was once a borderline fantasy ace, but Castillo is now merely solid as he enters his age-32 season.

Paredes was traded twice in the final sixth months of 2024, first to the Cubs and later to the Astros in the Kyle Tucker deal. The power dipped after his move from Tampa Bay to the North Side, but his new home in Houston looks like a great fit for Paredes' pull-heavy approach from the right side. Indeed the Crawford Boxes could help Paredes return to the 30-homer plateau, but a career .245 BABIP saddles him with a low batting average and speaks to his limited running ability. His batted-ball profile is not what one might expect, though Paredes is a unique player and the rules don't always apply to a hitter with his spray chart. The third baseman carries bonus first-base eligibility in leagues with a 15-game minimum.

Tasked with taking over the No. 1 starter role for Milwaukee following Corbin Burnes' departure via trade, Peralta performed admirably in 2024, albeit not quite to the level of his ace predecessor. His strikeout and walk rates went in the wrong direction and he had some issues with the long ball, particularly at home, allowing 1.72 HR/9 at American Family Field. Peralta also had trouble the third time through the order, posting a 7.52 ERA, a far cry from the 3.86 mark he posted the third time through in 2023. Nonetheless, he reached double-digit wins for the third time in four seasons as the Brewers ran away with the NL Central. While he may be miscast as an ace, Peralta has reached 30 starts and 200 strikeouts in back-to-back seasons. He totaled a career-high 173.2 innings last year and will be a bargain for the team at an $8 million price tag for 2025.

On the mend from his second career Tommy John surgery -- his first was in college in 2016, while this one was in August 2023 -- McClanahan should be eased back into the rotation gently by the always cautious Rays. Before the operation, he had developed into one of the game's best at his craft, with his 3.02 ERA and 33.4% whiff rates both ranking top-10 among pitchers with at least 50 starts from 2021-23. Whether McClanahan can quickly snap back to those levels is unclear, but if he's looking good during spring training and on track for the Opening Day rotation, he'd be a potential top-30 fantasy starter.

Few relievers made as many gains in 2024 as Jax. He added more than a half-mph to his average fastball velocity, significantly boosted the whiff rate on his sweeper and lowered his walk rate to 5.4%, with the result being the 10th-highest fantasy point total among relief pitchers (closers or middle relief). Jax thrived in his eighth-inning role, additionally securing 10 saves, and in most every regard outperformed closer Jhoan Duran in the process. That's not to say that a closer competition is destined this spring, but considering manager Rocco Baldelli's preference for matchups-oriented relief roles, Jax should put forth meaningful, nearly top-10 RP fantasy stats, regardless of how he's used.

Gil had a breakout campaign in 2024 with a 3.50 ERA, 1.19 WHIP and 171:77 K:BB across 151.2 innings, which narrowly won him the American League Rookie of the Year Award. The right-hander had a 1.99 ERA through the first two months of the season but labored during the summer months and posted a 4.58 ERA the rest of the way. Walks were a concern during both of those periods -- his 77 walks were the most among all MLB pitchers -- which is hardly a surprise since that was a consistent issue through his minor-league career. Gil showcased his strikeout potential with a 10.1 K/9 and has room for growth with just 36 big-league starts under his belt, but he'll likely need to cut down on the walks in order to stave off regression, let alone take a meaningful step forward in his second full season.

The Astros gave Altuve a vote of long-term confidence last February in the form of a five-year extension and he rewarded their continued faith with a 20-20 season, his first such season since 2017. Altuve earned his ninth All-Star selection with a .306 average and 14 homers in the first half before dipping to .277 and six, respectively, in the second half. The second baseman has always made the most of his talents and continues to take advantage of the Crawford Boxes in Houston, slugging more than 100 points higher at home versus on the road last season. Gone are the days of first-round value, but Altuve can still provide well-round production, with his greatest contributions at this stage coming in runs and batting average. Altuve, nearing his 35th birthday in May, has been mostly healthy in recent years outside of 2023 when he missed nearly half the season with thumb and oblique injuries.

Abreu is the only reliever in baseball to have struck out 100 or more batters out of the bullpen in each of the past two seasons, joining teammate Josh Hader as well as Fernando Cruz and Mason Miller in that club for 2024. Abreu could challenge for saves on most other clubs, but as long as he and Hader are teammates, Abreu appears to be the Robin to Hader's Batman. Abreu has the highest strikeout rate among all non-closing relievers over the past three seasons, and those strikeouts and stellar ratios make Abreu an interesting play in deep formats. The risk comes in the fact that so few relievers ever work 70-plus innings over consecutive seasons let alone three as Abreu will likely be asked to do with Houston dealing Ryan Pressly away this winter.

Greene, the No. 5 overall pick of the 2019 amateur draft and a top-10 overall prospect entering his 2022 rookie season, has made incremental gains across his three MLB campaigns to date. Unfortunately, those have also included extensive -- though generally unlucky -- absences, from the fractured right foot that delayed his arrival in Detroit in 2022, to the fractured left fibula that cost him five weeks of 2023, the Tommy John surgery that prematurely ended his 2023 in early September and the hamstring strain that cost him three weeks last summer. When healthy, Greene's contact-quality metrics are stellar, akin to those you'd expect from an All-Star. With some better fortune in the injury department, he could be ready to join the top-50 players in fantasy baseball in 2025.

Baz began the season with Triple-A Durham, starting 10 games but only logging 39.1 innings. After being called up in early July, Baz started 14 games spanning 79.1 frames. His 3.06 ERA with the Rays looks effective, but a 4.39 xFIP and 4.33 SIERA paint a different picture. Baz's strikeout rate was way down while his walk rate was up relative to his pre-injury levels. Throwing 118.2 combined innings last season suggests Baz can handle a bump into the 150-170 range, and considering that he was able to reach back for more zip at times last season, it's reasonable to think he may be able to add velocity  in 2025. A return to pre-injury form and the top of the rotation is in play, but don't expect ace production right away.

Kopech successfully made the transition back to the bullpen after a two-year run of working in the White Sox rotation. Kopech saved nine games on the South Side before being dealt to Los Angeles for Miguel Vargas, and he became a dominant piece in the Dodgers' bullpen as they went on to win it all. The addition of Tanner Scott this offseason very much changes the outlook on Kopech, since it now looks like it will be tough for him to get to double-digit saves, though he will certainly still be part of the back-end mix. Kopech, even in a non-closing capacity, should be able to help with ratios and strikeouts while vulturing wins much like Blake Treinen did last season in front of Kopech, Daniel Hudson and Evan Phillips. The lack of saves will push down Kopech's immediate value, but this would be a pricy in-season acquisition should anything happen to Scott.

It appeared that Detmers' long-awaited breakthrough was happening early in 2024, as he recorded a 3.12 ERA and 1.15 WHIP after five starts. Unfortunately, the script suddenly flipped, and he logged a 9.85 ERA and 1.87 WHIP over his next six outings. Detmers was then demoted to Triple-A Salt Lake, but he to make five starts in September and struggled with an 8.14 ERA and 1.77 WHIP. His 3.86 xFIP and 27.9% strikeout rate offer some room for optimism, but Detmers needs more consistent command and control. Still just 25 years old, there are worse speculative plays, but Detmers will have to earn an Opening Day rotation spot after the Angels fortified their staff with Yusei Kikuchi and Kyle Hendricks.

One of the game's highest risk/reward players, Lewis has missed more Twins games over the past two seasons (172) than he has played during his three-year MLB career, yet in those 152 games played he has 33 HR and 104 RBI. He's still only 25 years old, with plenty of career left in which to shake his growing reputation for being injury prone, but at the same time, fellow Twin Byron Buxton had a similar penchant for absences that he was never able to shake. Lewis certainly possesses the ability to be one of the best at his position, but drafting him requires a leap of faith.

After struggling with home runs and the command of his fastball as a rookie, Bradley made big strides in 2024 that bode well for his future. He boosted his ground-ball rate by 6%, added more than 2% to his whiff rate, and rattled off a final 20 starts in which his ERA was 3.71 and he generated MLB's 11th-most strikeouts (122). Considering Bradley's prospect status, it was a signal that he might begin to realize his future ace potential in 2025. The Rays do tend to take a conservative approach with their young starters' innings, and their move from pitchers' heaven Tropicana Field to George M. Steinbrenner Field sets them back slightly. Still, Bradley should be drafted in the middle rounds based upon his upside.

Kiley McDaniel's No. 29 overall prospect entering last season, Lee fell well short of expectations during his rookie campaign, hampered by back and biceps injuries while posting mediocre-at-best contact quality metrics. He'll be in the mix for the Twins' second base job in the best-case scenario, a utility role at his median, and a fill-in role behind the team's many injury-prone infielders on the low end. Lee seems most likely to contribute in the batting average category as he matures. He'll need to excel in Grapefruit League play to be anything more than a late-round mixed flier.

A consistently excellent all-around player despite playing under a relatively small spotlight in Cleveland, Ramirez should be a first-round pick in fantasy leagues of all types. He's the only player to have finished among the top 25 on our Player Rater as well as in total fantasy points scored in each of the past five seasons. In four of those, he finished among the top eight in each, and across that five-year span his 2,118 fantasy points were second only to Shohei Ohtani's 3,151. What's more, in 2024, Ramirez finished just one home run shy of becoming the second-oldest member of the 40/40 club (Barry Bonds, age 31, 1996), a signal that he still has plenty to offer fantasy managers. He's among the safest investments you'll find.

A big, powerful prospect, albeit one with a good amount of swing-and-miss in his game, Wood should make a sizable leap in the home run category in 2025. After hitting 26 homers in 129 minor league games in 2023, then another 10 in 52 games for Triple-A Rochester to begin last season, he arrived in Washington to deliver what would have been 95th-percentile-or-better exit velocity and hard-hit rates. Wood will need to get more lift in his swing to realize his massive home run potential -- his ground-ball rate was 55% as a rookie -- but between that possibility and the above-average speed that has helped him average 18 steals across four professional seasons, he'll be plenty appealing as a breakthrough pick in rotisserie leagues as is. Consider him in the middle rounds.

Amidst a bevy of talented, fastball-throwing frontline starters in Seattle, Gilbert has quietly emerged as a prospective ace. He has made noticeable gains in numerous statistical categories over the past two seasons, including WHIP, walk, strikeout, whiff and ground ball rates. Plus, he has cut roughly a half a run from his Statcast expected ERA in both of those campaigns. Gilbert's addition of a splitter in 2023 helped him become a more strikeout-oriented starter, and his move to a six-pitch repertoire with less fastball reliance in 2024 helped further diversify his skill set. While the Mariners offense probably hasn't improved to the point that he'll significantly boost last year's nine wins, Gilbert should again deliver excellent numbers otherwise. He's a solid fantasy building block.

No longer is Gallen being drafted as a borderline ace. He missed roughly a month of the 2024 season with a hamstring injury and his walk rate increased by more than three percentage points, which led to his WHIP jumping from 1.12 to 1.26. Gallen's knuckle curve remains an excellent put-away pitch, but his four-seam fastball and slider were entirely hittable last season. Perhaps Gallen has fallen further than he should. After all, the right-hander was a Cy Young finalist in the National League in 2023, he won 14 games in a down year and still does a lot well relative to most starting pitchers in MLB, including limiting homers. Take the name away and the underlying profile is not all that exciting, but Gallen's numbers over the last three years give him a case to be viewed as a third or fourth starter in fantasy entering 2025.

Webb continues to be one of the game's most durable and reliable starters, despite fanning hitters at a below-average clip. Control and command remain Webb's bread and butter, along with an extreme groundball rate. His 613 innings since 2022 lead the majors, but his 529 strikeouts over that span rank 15th. Webb's ERA and WHIP are both top 10 among all starters with at least 500 innings over the past three seasons, but both are vulnerable to variance since Webb allows so many balls in play. Feeding into the concern is the fact that Webb's swinging-strike rate has declined each of the past three seasons. Accepting the low strikeout discount on Webb has been a fruitful endeavor, but it's reached the point where doing so invites more risk than may be evident by recent performance.

Olson was not exempt from the seemingly team-wide funk that struck the 2024 Braves. He posted his worst OPS and OPS-plus as well as his worst strikeout, walk, home run, hard-hit and Statcast Barrel rates since the abbreviated 2020 campaign, although his cumulative numbers wound up looking eerily similar to his 2022 effort. His 2024 looked unusually unlucky and the fact he finished the year on a .282/.380/.573, 16-HR flourish across the Braves' final 60 games suggests that he'll rebound to a degree. Olson was effectively a top-40 overall player in points leagues and a top-70 rotisserie perforner in 2021-22, which seems like a fair valuation for what to expect from him in 2025.

One of baseball's most consistent power sources, but also one of its most free-swinging hitters, Hernandez has hit 25-plus homers in each of the last five full MLB seasons and 32-plus in two of his last four. By returning to the Dodgers this winter, he chose to remain in one of the game's better home run environments, as well as one of its most potent lineups. Hernandez should again deliver value akin to his 2024, which had him a top-25 rotisserie and top-75 overall points league performer.

Albies is a three-time All-Star and two-time Silver Slugger, but injuries have kept him under 100 games played in two of the past three seasons. First, a fractured right toe put him on the shelf last year before a fractured left wrist cost him most of the summer. There was some uncertainty as to whether he would return last season, but Albies made it back for nine games at the very end of the campaign. In addition to the injuries, there have been chirps that Albies could or perhaps should give up switch hitting given his career splits as a left-handed hitter against right-handed pitching (.247/.309/.434). Despite the flaws in his profile, Albies is arguably still right up there among the top second basemen on the board, maybe behind only Ketel Marte. As he enters his age-28 season, Albies will be attempting to turn the page on his recent health woes and return to 30-10 production for Atlanta.

Reynolds is a textbook Professional Hitter coming off four straight 20-homer seasons and back-to-back 20-10 campaigns. His batting average has not fallen below .260 in a full season and Reynolds has been an All-Star in two of the past four years since his fluke down year in 2020. While his defense in the outfield corners has fallen off a cliff, the Pirates have not seemed to mind nor have they indicated a positional change could be in the cards. Reynolds signed an eight-year contract extension in 2023 and will return to anchor the heart of the Pittsburgh order after batting exclusively out of the two hole last season -- typically where teams put their best hitter. Entering his age-30 season, Reynolds provides a stable floor in terms of skills and playing time.

O'Hoppe struck out nearly 30 percent of the time last season, but overall he was a bright spot for a last-place Angels squad, hitting 20 homers and providing plus value behind the plate. After missing a large chunk of 2023 with a shoulder injury, O'Hoppe seemed to hit a wall in August of last season, posting a .339 OPS that month before rebounding to .791 in September. Drafted in the 23rd round out of high school in 2018, O'Hoppe has proven to be a tremendous find and developmental success story for the organization. The strikeouts should be manageable with his batted-ball profile, and improvement against left-handed pitching seems likely given his 2023 numbers. Entering his age-25 season, O'Hoppe appears capable of jumping a tier or two at the catcher position while playing his home games at a park that is generally favorable for right-handed power.

While Ryan has established himself as a quality starting pitcher in Major League Baseball, injuries have delayed the full-on breakout. He went down in August with a Grade 2 teres major strain and never made it back onto the field last season, though the Twins said in November that Ryan was making good progress in his recovery. A groin injury derailed his 2023 season, but through it all the right-hander has made 79 starts over the past three seasons (31st in the majors in that span). His flyball tendencies make him susceptible to homers, but Ryan is stingy with walks and misses bats at an above-average clip with his five-pitch mix. More cautious players will want to wait and see how Ryan looks in the spring before jumping in with both feet while those with a higher level of risk tolerance should be eager to invest in the skills.

Defense doesn't count in fantasy baseball scoring, but Crow-Armstrong's highlight reel glovework helps keep his bat in the lineup. He hits the ball with more authority than others that are reliant on steals for fantasy purposes, but he strikes out more and lacks patience. Crow-Armstrong also hits more fly balls than a typical speed merchant. A lot must come together, but Crow-Armstrong has the makings of a fantasy star, though that's not likely in 2025. He must first learn to make better swing decisions, so he can best blend his power and speed potential. For now, consider Crow-Armstrong a source of cheap steals, but be prepared to absorb a low batting average.

Duran is coming off a second consecutive 20-plus-save season, though his role in the Minnesota bullpen has been somewhat in fluid, more so than fantasy managers would like. As a rookie in 2022, he blew batters away with an 18.1 percent swinging-strike rate and an elite strikeout-minus-walk percentage. However, he has not been able to achieve the same level of overall success over the past two seasons. This past year saw a reduction in his strikeout rate while opponents hit 28 points higher against Duran. He also struggled to prevent runners from scoring when they got on base. It feels like a pitcher with this much swing and miss and such a high groundball rate should have better outcomes than what Duran has earned to date. The expected stats show what Duran's is capable of.

Abbott was limited to 25 starts after his season ended in mid-August due to a strained shoulder, but he's expected to be healthy for spring training. His 3.72 ERA is misleading as shown by a less impressive 4.91 xFIP and 4.78 SIERA. A high 82.9% left on base mark rescued his season. Abbott's strikeout rate plummeted to 19.5%, down from 26.1% in his rookie season. His velocity and repertoire didn't change, so perhaps Abbott needs to be less predictable with his sequencing.
