He's slated to be in the Reds rotation, but unless he regains lost dominance, Abbott's ratios are vulnerable, particularly at home in Great American Ballpark.

Garcia played in 157 games last year, but he holds the dubious distinction of his 69 wRC+ being the lowest among all qualified hitters. Fortunately, he swiped 37 bags, the seventh most in MLB. His game is putting the ball in play, mostly on the ground. His Hard-Hit rate and average exit velocity are above average, but not stout enough to supply much pop in power-suppressing Kauffman Stadium. Garcia is not a patient batter, so his time at or near the top of the order are likely over, especially with Jonathan India and a healthy Vinnie Pasquantino in tow. Even though Garcia's skills and defense are best suited for a utility role, he's slated to man the hot corner again in 2025. Even so, relying on Garcia for steals is a slippery slope, since someone else, such as Cavan Biggio, could cut into Garcia's playing time. Having dual second and third base eligibility sweetens Garcia's charm as a streamer in daily formats.

Correa was an elite producer in 2024 with a .310/.388/.517 slash line, but the catch is he was limited to just 86 games due to plantar fasciitis in his right foot. He dealt with the same injury in his other foot in 2023, though he still played in 135 games while laboring to a .711 OPS. Correa returned to action for the final weeks of the 2024 regular season and raked despite still being clearly hobbled, but he's expected to begin spring training in good health. Now entering his age-30 campaign, the injury questions will only intensify for Correa, who has played 150 games in a season just once in his big-league career. That being said, he played in at least 130 contests the previous three seasons, with the extended absence last year being his first lengthy stay on the IL since 2019. Correa will likely be a major fantasy asset if he can stay healthy, but that's a significant "if" for the shortstop at this stage of his career.

A cornerstone of the Nationals' rebuild, Crews, the No. 2 overall pick of the 2023 draft, has all of the tools necessary to develop into an eventual rotisserie and points-based fantasy star. His contact-oriented swing and blazing speed were most apparent during his 2024 MLB debut (albeit more rewarded in roto formats), but his contact quality metrics bodes well for his eventually adding enough power to help more in points leagues. Crews will need to curb his 56.4% ground ball rate in order to truly break through, but he's off to a good start to his career. He warrants a mid-round selection in redraft leagues and is a near-building block selection in dynasty formats.

Riley entered 2024 as one of the most consistent hitters in baseball with three straight 30-homer, 90-RBI seasons and an .878 OPS during that span, but he underwhelmed last year with a .256/.322/.461 slash line and 19 home runs through 110 games before a fractured hand ended his campaign in mid-August. Despite the drop in production, the veteran third baseman was still making consistent hard contact, which bodes well for a rebound in 2025. He should have a fairly typical offseason given the timing of the injury, so there's no real question on his status heading into spring training. Riley's .783 OPS in a down season illustrates his high floor, and there's a strong likelihood he bounces back to his All-Star form in 2025 given his track record and the fact he'll turn just 28 years old in April.

Alonso is 30, coming off a season with a career-high 42% ground-ball rate, and his free agency lingered deep into the offseason. All of this spawns concerns about his fantasy value that hadn't previously been present. He remains one of the game's premier power sources, hitting 34 home runs in 2024, making him the only player with at least that many in each of the past five full MLB seasons, but other aspects of his game have begun trending in the wrong direction. In the right environment, Alonso might yet have more seasons within range of his 2022-23 output in his bat, but his downside is beginning to deepen. Consider him to be an early- to mid-round pick, but he's no longer the fantasy building block he once was.

Butler used up his rookie eligibility in 2023 and had a .582 OPS in 42 games, but he was electric during his first full MLB campaign last year with 22 homers, 18 steals and a .262/.317/.490 slash line in 125 contests. He still endured some ups and downs, however, as he was demoted to Triple-A in May after posting a .555 OPS through 121 plate appearances. Butler rejoined the Athletics in mid-June and was one of the best hitters in baseball the rest of the way, and he clubbed 20 home runs in his final 84 games. The underlying numbers back up the production, so there shouldn't be any major worries about regression in 2025. Butler clearly has the potential to deliver a 20-20 campaign, and the move from The Coliseum in Oakland to the more hitter-friendly Sutter Health Park in Sacramento should help him build on the breakout season.

Adames parlayed what was a career year on many fronts into a seven-year, $182 million contract with the Giants -- one of the offseason's earliest signings. He'll now play in a more challenging hitting environment than during his three and a half years in Milwaukee. Playing in the Brewers' HR-friendly home ballpark, Adames managed personal bests with his 32 home runs, 112 RBI, 93 runs scored, 153 hits, 33 doubles, 21 stolen bases, 74 walks and 282 total bases last season, while also pacing all major leaguers with 224 plate appearances and 93 RBI with runners in scoring position. The park switch assures some regression in the power departments, as does the good fortune in the RBI column. Nevertheless, Adames is a prime-age hitter who should put forth top-10 positional numbers in all fantasy formats.

From a pure baseball perspective, it's a shame that Trout's career has trended downwards from one-time contender for "best player in baseball history" to merely a certain first-ballot Hall of Famer. Injuries have been a persistent problem for him across the last eight seasons, but especially the past four, during which he has missed more Angels games while on the IL (360) than he has played (266). Those ailments, and probably also the aging curve (he's now 33) have diminished his once-blazing speed as well as begun to erode his top-shelf contact quality. Even accounting for all that, Trout is still one of the game's most stellar talents. This guy, after all, hit 10 homers across his first 25 games of 2024. His power and patience remain his most marketable fantasy skills, ideal for points-based and sabermetric scoring, but Trout is more of a mid- than early-round pick these days with the many questions surrounding his durability.

After leading the majors in plate appearances for three consecutive years, Semien finished fourth last season with 718. His numbers were down across the board, though he still cracked 23 homers and reached triple digits in runs scored as the Rangers' primary leadoff hitter. Manager Bruce Bochy hinted in December that Semien, now 34, could get more days off in 2025 and beyond, and also said that he has floated the idea of moving Semien around the batting order. Semien has been barely above a .300 OBP in two of the past three years, so the move would be justified, but that combination of more days off and a lower spot in the order could wreak havoc on the second baseman's counting stats. His plate skills are holding steady and he can still run a bit, but Semien is trending in the wrong direction and the track record carries a bit less weight at this stage.

Raleigh set new personal bests with 34 home runs and 100 RBI last season, finishing as the No. 2 catcher in traditional fantasy leagues despite a .220 batting average. The switch-hitting backstop has become a folk hero of sorts in Seattle with his majestic homers and timely hitting among other reasons. The fact that he's a significant plus behind the plate with his defense and framing helps Raleigh's chances of approaching or exceeding 600 plate appearances for the Mariners once again in 2025. The drain in batting average is significant but does not negate the value of his power and counting stats, which get a scarcity bump in two-catcher formats. Expect more of the same in 2025 with Raleigh overcoming the pitcher-friendly skew of his home ballpark.

After giving up eight earned runs over 1.1 innings in his 2024 debut, Ober went on an incredible run in which he went 12-4 with a 3.05 ERA and 0.92 WHIP over 138.1 innings, before hitting the skids again at the end of the season. Overall, it was an impressive showing for the 6-foot-9 righty as he solidified his standing in the middle of the Minnesota rotation. He has four quality pitches and his strikeout and walk rates are good enough to make up for the occasional bout of gopheritis. The disappointing end to the season (0-4, 5.59 ERA in his final seven starts) may be enough to keep the more casual drafters away, but the secret is out amongst the wider drafting public. Chances are, the home runs will persist given his flyball tendencies, but Ober is good enough to overcome them and reach double-digit wins once again for a competitive Twins team.

His status as a shortstop/closer during his college days at Nebraska, coupled with the 2021 Tommy John surgery that delayed the start of his professional career, perhaps allowed Schwellenbach to sneak beneath the radar entering 2024. The Braves, desperate for rotation options, gave him a look in late May, despite his having only made two starts as high as Double-A ball at the time. He never looked back. Schwellenbach finished 16th among starting pitchers in fantasy points, thanks to his five solid pitch offerings and an elite walk rate (his 4.6% ranked in the 95th percentile). While he's likely to regress somewhat as the league becomes more familiar with him, he has the skills to remain a top-40 fantasy starter if given the innings (he totaled 168 2/3 between the majors and minors in 2024).

The 2024 season was a disaster for Strider and his fantasy managers, as the No. 1 pitcher off most draft boards lasted just two starts before succumbing to season-ending elbow surgery -- though he had an internal brace procedure this time after having Tommy John surgery previously in 2019. That gives the right-hander hope of returning in the early stages of 2025. Stiil, there is always risk of setbacks or diminished performance in pitchers initially returning from such a significant operation. When healthy, Strider has been the game's best strikeout artist -- his 458 K's across his span of 54 healthy starts from May 2022-April 2024 were 51 more than the next-closest hurler -- so he'll naturally slide in as one of this year's top risk/reward pitcher picks. Monitor his rehabilitation throughout spring training, as his prognosis could drive his draft value as high as a top-25 SP pick or more of a late-round flier.

The Yankees' big hitting acquisition following Juan Soto's free-agent departure, Bellinger brings his pull-power, fly ball-oriented swing to Yankee Stadium -- possibly the best fit yet for his skill set. Though Bellinger's contact-quality metrics have been below-average for four years running, he gets the most out of his swings, and his improved contact over the last two seasons gives him as much of a chance at contributing batting average as well as home runs. A rebound to his 2023 norms might be a stretch, but it's not entirely out of the question in pinstripes. He's well worth a mid-round selection.

Suarez delivered in his first season as the Padres' regular closer, converting 36 of 42 save chances. It's slightly concerning that half of Suarez's blown saves came in September, a month during which he posted a 6.00 ERA and 1.50 WHIP. However, he shook it off and logged three saves in the final week of the season and then two more in the playoffs. Suarez's strikeout rate isn't dominant, especially for a closer, but last season his 6.2 percent walk rate was the fourth lowest among relievers with at least 20 saves. Suarez is the favorite for saves in San Diego, but last year was his first fully healthy season and he'll be 34 years old in 2025, so rostering setup man Jason Adam in tandem with Suarez may be a wise move.

Munoz enters the 2025 season in a slightly different situation from just one year ago. He was not the clearcut favorite for the primary closer role last spring after the acquisition of Gregory Santos from the White Sox as well as the impressive work from Matt Brash in 2023. Yet, Munoz was the last man standing and he is now the clear frontrunner for saves in Seattle. He managed to avoid the injured list last season despite dealing with some back issues, earning an appearance in the All-Star Game. Munoz has twice now posted ERAs below 2.50 and WHIPs below 1.00 in the past three seasons, and the outstanding Seattle rotation and suspect offense almost ensure that there will be many late and close opportunities for Munoz to finally get to 30 saves in 2025.

Considering the number of injuries that dogged him -- elbow trouble that cost him the first six weeks, forearm discomfort that cost him a June start, and a hamstring strain that sidelined him for 2 1/2 weeks in July -- Woo's 2024, which earned him a top-30 SP valuation in roto formats, was rather surprising. He has some of the best control in baseball, his 2.8% walk rate was best in baseball among those with at least 100 IP, and he had a 2.95 ERA over his last 29 big-league starts. Still, Woo's elbow and forearm issues raise future concerns about his durability. Monitor him carefully during spring training, but with better injury luck, he should deliver top-50 fantasy SP value.

Happ tied a career high with 25 home runs in 2024 and also set career bests in runs (89) and RBI (86), while his .782 OPS remained in line with his marks from the previous two seasons. The veteran outfielder also recorded double-digit steals (13) for the second consecutive campaign, which he didn't accomplish in his first six big-league seasons. He continues to showcase his patience and finished tied-fifth in MLB with 80 walks, and he has a double-digit walk rate in four of the past five years. Happ has also won three straight Gold Gloves in left field for the Cubs, which helps him stick in the lineup through any slumps. He's played in nearly 96 percent of Chicago's games over the past five years and has provided a consistently above-average bat throughout his career, so Happ should be a reliable target for fantasy managers in 2025.

Though his control issues still crop up from time to time, Scott's skills have taken gargantuan steps forward over the past two seasons. Among relievers with at least 100 IP over that time, his 2.04 ERA ranks second, his 188 strikeouts rank fourth, his 69 saves plus holds ranks fifth and his .186 BAA comes in at seventh. Scott has also proven his durability by amassing the fourth-most relief innings over that time (150), something the Dodgers surely valued as they signed him to deepen their already strong late-inning relief corps. While the left-hander brings some volatility in the WHIP category, he should be a premium source of holds and/or saves. He should be one of the first relievers off your draft board once the proven, top-shelf closers are gone.

Rays manager Kevin Cash has a reputation for spreading the wealth when it comes to save chances, but Fairbanks has been the skipper's go-to arm in the ninth inning when available over the past two seasons. Fairbanks recorded 20-plus saves for the second straight year before a right lat strain ended his 2024 season, adding another chapter to his sketchy health history. Even with all the injuries in his career, Fairbanks continues to pump gas with 93rd percentile fastball velocity, though that didn't translate to many strikeouts in 2024. For now, Fairbanks can still be considered Tampa Bay's primary closer, but that run could be coming to an end in the not-too-distant future given his price tag for 2026 and the fact that he has incentives based on games finished in 2025.

Sanchez impressed by going 11-9 with a 3.32 ERA and 1.24 WHIP across 181.2 innings last season, his first as a full-time member of the Philadelphia rotation. The lefty's game is built around the sinking fastball which was the main driver in a 57.4 percent groundball rate last season, third highest among qualified starters. In turn, he allowed just 11 homers for the third-best HR/9 among that group. Sanchez can also pull the string on a changeup and spin a breaking ball, though the package has not included many strikeouts to date. It's possible that Sanchez, still just 28 years old, could unlock another level with the strikeouts, but that should not be expected since there is little reason to mess with a formula that has been largely successful. The K rate as it stands now caps his upside, but Sanchez looks like a viable pick to fill out any fantasy rotation in 2025.

One of the game's best hit-tool prospects, Wilson posted a .412 batting average and 97% contact rate in his final college season at Grand Canyon, .333/89% numbers in his 26-game pro debut in 2023, and .433/.93% numbers as a minor leaguer in 2024. That earned him a mid-July promotion to the Athletics, where he unfortunately suffered a hamstring injury in his MLB debut that cost him the next five weeks. Wilson returned to record similarly strong contact metrics as the team's starting shortstop down the stretch, and he figures to serve in the same role to begin 2025. He's lacking in much else at this stage of his career, but this is the kind of high-floor player mixed-leaguers should want from their middle infield spot.

Irvin's 33 starts tied for most in the majors last season, as he pitched a career-high 187.2 innings. His 4.41 ERA was a tad high according to a 4.03 xFIP and 4.21 SIERA. With a low 20.3 percent strikeout rate, Irvin is more susceptible to variance, which is amplified by a high home run rate. Irvin improved his strikeout and walk rates last season and is just 28 years old, so he could continue to improve. The Nationals are also developing something of a reputation for developing pitching. The safe play is paying for the floor and deploying Irvin sagely, avoiding power-laden lineups.

Crawford was coming off a 2023 season in which he smacked a career-best 19 homers with a .380 on-base percentage, fueled by his best walk rate in a full season and leading to nearly 100 runs scored. Last season, a fractured pinky was an issue in the middle of the summer, but Crawford was only hitting .204/.296/.347 with a 22.8 percent strikeout rate prior to the injury. He returned at the end of August but finished with a .194/.319/.245 line the rest of the way. Perhaps the lesson learned here is what goes up must come down, but Crawford had never struggled to this level since his first season in Seattle back in 2019. The challenge with Crawford is he does not have a single fantasy skill to bank on, so he either rebounds by batted-ball fortune and moves back up the lineup or hits ninth and lives on the waiver wire.

In this era with a dwindling number of aces, Wheeler is a relative rarity. He and teammate Aaron Nola are the only pitchers to have made at least 30 starts and totaled 190-plus IP as many as four times over the past six seasons. Since the beginning of 2019, Wheeler's 2,413 fantasy points rank second, his 108 quality starts first, his 1,024 2/3 innings rank second, his 1,094 strikeouts third, his 3.14 ERA ninth and his 1.07 WHIP 10th. He also set personal bests as a 34-year-old in 2024 with his 2.57 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, .191 BAA and 26 quality starts, further signaling his skill set rating as one of the most stable at the position. Wheeler is a pitcher around whom you build your fantasy team.

Cruz is making good on the hype and there is still room for growth as he enters his age-26 season. He cracked 21 homers and swiped 22 bags in 23 attempts last year, showcasing his loud tools and athleticism. There were some lingering issues with his left ankle after he missed nearly all of 2023 with a fracture, but the Pirates have said that they do not expect the ankle to be a long-term concern. The team moved him from shortstop to center field in late August, which seemed rather sudden at the time although it was not entirely unexpected given Cruz was always an anomaly as a 6-foot-7 shortstop. A strikeout rate over 30 percent for his career gives him some downside in batting average, but optimists can reasonably dream on another level of upside in home runs and stolen bases in 2025.

Naylor set career highs in games played, plate appearances, homers, runs and RBI last season. Volume was clearly a factor, but a career-high ISO was also a major contributor. Naylor needed the boost in power since he was unable to maintain the prior season's batted-ball fortune. The power spike could be fleeting for a number of reasons. Above all, Chase Field in Arizona, his new home venue, suppresses lefty power unlike his old digs in Cleveland which amplifies left-handed pop. A low strikeout rate and a projected spot in the middle of the Diamondbacks' order give Naylor a draftable floor, but plan on a modest power decline.

Eovaldi went a long way in shedding the fragility label by throwing his second-highest innings total last season. He will miss a start from time to time, as he has but twice made 30 starts, but when he is out there, he works deep into games thanks to his ability to throw four different pitches to lefties and five to righties. The repertoire is a bit susceptible to the long ball, but Eovaldi's stinginess with walks offsets the damage from those homers. He is one of just six pitchers to have posted an ERA of 4.00 and a WHIP below 1.25 while pitching at least 100 innings in each of the past four seasons, joining the likes of Framber Valdez, Corbin Burnes, Kevin Gausman, Logan Webb and Zack Wheeler. That's good company to keep.

Yamamoto, one of the most ballyhooed Japanese arrivals of the past decade-plus, had a U.S. debut season that will be regarded by most as a disappointment. From the five runs in just a single inning's work he surrendered in his big-league debut last March, to the near-three months he missed due to a triceps injury, he never got much of an extended chance to showcase his tremendous raw stuff. Yamamoto did, however, enjoy a 12-start stretch with a 2.41 ERA and 28.5% strikeout rate, and his four-seam fastball, splitter and curveball each registered excellent marks. The ingredients of a staff ace -- granted one subject to the six-man rotation and a probable innings cap -- are still here.

Suarez made the most of his change of scenery and had his best season at the plate since 2019. That 2019 season will not be replicated, but for Suarez to hit 30 homers and drive in 100-plus in a neutral offensive environment with baseballs that were not traveling as far last year says something. Suarez continues to be a fastball destroyer and he remains quite capable of punishing mistakes. The third baseman still has a good amount of swing and miss in his game, which can lead to some serious peaks and valleys. To that point, he had just 10 homers and a .216/.302/.366 line at the All Star break last season. Suarez hitting 20 homers with a .307/.341/.602 line in the second half won some leagues and quieted the doubters who thought 2023 was the start of an acceleration into the aging curve.

Kelly's two-year run of success was derailed in 2024 by a teres major strain to his throwing shoulder which put him on the shelf from mid-April to mid-August. Arizona was happy enough with the results and confident enough in the health of his shoulder to exercise Kelly's $7 million club option for the 2025 season. He is such an unusual starting pitcher these days because his traditional fastball was his tertiary pitch by usage rate last season, with Kelly instead emphasizing his cutter and changeup. Kelly, like many pitchers in their mid-30s, has had to adjust his repertoire as his velocity has waned, and the changeup in particular has helped in recent seasons. The changeup to lefties and the slider to righties are his preferred put-away pitches, but his strikeout rate fell to below average last year around his recovery from the shoulder strain.

This is the Lowe whose name rhymes with "ow," reflecting his six trips to the IL across the past three seasons alone, for back (three), triceps, knee and oblique issues, totaling 162 missed Rays games. Between the absences, Lowe has continued to show elite-to-top-shelf raw power metrics, and his 5.2% home run rate across the last five seasons leads all second basemen. That ability makes him too good to completely ignore in mixed leagues, though selecting him demands a strong backup plan.

A decently regarded prospect back in his Dodgers/Athletics days nearly a decade ago, Holmes finally reached the majors last June at the age of 28, parlaying his elite control and whiff-generating slider and curveball into a swingman role with the Braves. His performance impressed them enough that he earned the start in their must-win Game 162 against the Mets, in which he tossed four shutout innings of 1-hit, 7-K baseball, and winter chatter had him as a likely member of their 2025 Opening Day rotation. Whether Holmes, who before last season's 109 1/3 combined innings between the majors and minors hadn't exceeded 90 frames since 2017, has the stamina to hold up to a full-season starter's role is in question, but he's an intriguing flier in deep mixed and NL-only formats.

Busch, a first-round pick by the Dodgers in 2019, was traded to the Cubs last winter, opening up a path to playing time at the major-league level. Busch took advantage and showed what he's made of with an above-average offensive season at age 26 that included 21 homers and a .775 OPS across 567 plate appearances. Best of all for his 2025 outlook, Busch handled same-side pitching capably, slashing .258/.330/.382 against left-handed pitching. That performance along with his defense at first base, which the Cubs see as Gold Glove caliber, figure to keep Busch in the lineup nearly every day. First base has become rather top heavy in fantasy baseball and Busch makes for a decent fallback option for those that end up waiting at the position.

In hindsight, Williams' 2024 appeared to be a significant step backward, as an elbow injury cost him the season's first three months and his ERA ballooned by nearly a run and a half. Still, he added nearly a full tick of velocity to his fastball, and his curveball served as a legitimate swing-and-miss offering. The ingredients remain here for Williams to develop into one of fantasy's better starters, though he does have work to do before earning draft status as such. Consider him in the final rounds of 12-team mixed leagues, particularly if he's looking good come March.

Singer, a first-round pick by the Royals back in 2018, was traded to the Reds this past November in exchange for Jonathan India and Joey Wiemer. The move from Kansas City to Cincinnati comes with a park downgrade, although it's not as significant as one might suspect, at least not in terms of overall run scoring. Great American Ball Park plays more favorably for power hitting, but Singer's heavy sinker approach should help mitigate that factor, at least in theory. He upped his strikeout rate last season and has shown decent swing-and-miss ability with his breaking pitches, though Singer's strikeout rate has typically hovered around league average. While he should be drafted as a streamer in 2025, Singer could emerge as a more regular option for fantasy managers if new skipper Terry Francona can push the right buttons and protect his leads.

Following his return from July 2023 elbow surgery -- an internal brace procedure, after he had twice previously had Tommy John surgery -- Rasmussen was eased back into action by the Rays, largely as a reliever. He acclimated himself well to the switch, reflecting spikes in his average fastball velocity and strikeout rate, which offers promise heading into 2025. Rasmussen should return to the Rays rotation to begin the year, but keep in mind that their conservative approach to pitching workloads means the right-hander might be looking at closer to a 120- than a 160-inning workload. Still, he has the skills to be an every-start fantasy option while available if his stuff looks as good in March as it did last September.

Smith's wRC+ declined for the fourth straight season, but his 111 mark was still one of the top efforts from a catcher, especially one with the sixth most plate appearances at the position. With Shohei Ohtani joining the Dodgers, Smith only served as the DH three times. However, there is evidence that his drop in production wasn't necessarily due to the extra games behind the plate. April was by far Smith's best month with a .397 wOBA, then the final five months fell between .279 and .332, with September being his second-best month. Since 2021, only Salvador Perez has had more plate appearances as a backstop and just J.T. Realmuto has caught more innings than Smith, so a gentle drop in exit velocity and Hard-Hit rate is understandable. Even so, Smith's quality and quantity of contact remain solid for the position, keeping Smith among the first backstops off the board.

What a breakthrough Duran's 2024 campaign was! Few players have made as many all-around strides as he has over the past three years. He set personal bests in most every statistical category -- many of them by substantial margins -- culminating in his finishing 13th on our Player Rater and 18th overall in fantasy points scored. Most importantly, Duran, once a defensive liability, managed the eighth-best Statcast Fielding Run Value among outfielders, his strength in that department very much behind his MLB-leading 735 plate appearances. That amount of playing time will be tough to replicate, meaning some pull-back in his numbers is to be expected. Still, as a top-of-the-order Red Sox hitter, Duran should remain a top-50 fantasy performer regardless of format.

Bednar appeared to be on the precipice of becoming a top-tier closer until his clumsy start to the 2024 season. Bednar posted an 11.70 ERA in the first month of the campaign, including three blown saves in the first two weeks. Bednar then went on to convert his next 11 consecutive chances from May 1 until an oblique injury sent him to the injured list in the middle of the summer. The right-hander returned just before the All-Star break but backslid to an 0-5 record with four blown saves in 11 chances, leading to his demotion from the closer role. By season's end, Bednar's strikeout rate had declined six full percentage points while his walk rate worsened another three percentage points. While Bednar is tentatively expected to return to the ninth in 2025, his hold on the job has to be considered extremely tenuous until he shows his health and command troubles are behind him.

Harris had a whirlwind season in 2024, going from a .304 batting average in the first month to a .200 average in May to landing on the injured list in June. His injury was classified as a Grade 2 strain of his left hamstring and the outfielder ended up shifting to the 60-day IL before returning in August. Harris ultimately bookended his campaign with an impressive month of September in which he slashed .316/.344/.579 with eight homers. He was regularly batting leadoff down the stretch and could very well remain there to begin 2025 with Ronald Acuna expected to miss at least the first month while recovering from knee surgery. A low walk rate threatens to relegate Harris back to the lower third eventually, but if he stays on the field he could finally reach 20-20 with Atlanta after falling just short in 2022 and 2023.

Abrams appeared in only 138 games last season, but half of the missed time occurred in September when he missed out on the last eight games of the season after being demoted to Triple-A for staying out all night prior to a day game. Despite a second-half swoon, Abrams improved his hard-hit rate overall and experienced an uptick in power. The added production helped mitigate a drop in steals. In 2023, Abrams swiped 47 bags in 51 tries for an outstanding 92 percent success rate. Last season, he was just 31-for-43 (72 percent). Still just 24 years old, Abrams is expected to learn from last season's disciplinary action and continue maturing as a person and player. The arrows are pointing upward, especially if he can cut down on last season's caught stealing number.

After four seasons serving as one of baseball's most unhittable relievers -- both his 1.75 ERA and .146 BAA from 2020-23 were easily best in the game -- Williams' 2024 swung his skill set into risk/reward territory. Back issues that plagued him late in 2023 resurfaced during spring training, costing him four months, but upon his return he hardly skipped a beat. Among pitchers with at least 20 IP following his July 28 activation, Williams' 43.2% strikeout rate ranked second, his 14 saves tied for fourth and his .133 BAA ranked 10th. The Yankees acquired him during the winter to take over as their closer, their confidence signaling more ?reward? to his fantasy calculus. If his back issues are indeed behind him, he'll make another run at the position's top spot.

Lopez is a legitimate frontline starter in Major League Baseball, if not quite a fantasy ace. The right-hander has been dependable, taking the ball 32 times and reaching 180 innings each of the past three seasons -- the last two with Minnesota. Always stingy with walks, Lopez shaved his walk rate to a career-low 5.3 percent last season, which helped him keep his WHIP below 1.20 for the fifth consecutive campaign. He has five different pitches, all of which can generate whiffs, though his changeup was not as effective in 2024. Regardless, Lopez found his groove in the second half, pitching to a 2.77 ERA in 81.1 innings after the break. While Lopez may not look like a particularly flashy upside pick, he misses enough bats and could easily return to All-Star status. He has often underperformed his estimators, though it's always possible he could have a year where the results beat the peripherals.

Greene was in the midst of a breakthrough 2024, posting nine wins, 13 quality starts, a 2.83 ERA, a 1.02 WHIP and 162 strikeouts through his first 24 starts, before right elbow soreness derailed the rest of his season. He did return in time to make two solid appearances in late September, but the absence added to what has been an alarming injury history in his young MLB career, including IL stints at least five weeks in length in each of his three seasons. Greene has long possessed front-of-the-rotation stuff and, with better luck in the health department, he might yet realize that status in 2025. He's a prospective top-30 fantasy starter with upside, well worth a pick in the middle rounds of your draft.

Recovery from Tommy John surgery cost Bautista the entirety of 2024, but baseball is expected to have its best reliever (at the time of the operation) back in time to close for the Orioles come Opening Day. In 2023, he registered the sixth-best strikeout rate (46.4%) of any pitcher with at least 60 IP, and became only the eighth pitcher in history with at least 30 saves, 110 strikeouts and a sub-1.50 ERA. Whether Bautista's raw stuff will approach those heights in his first season back following surgery is a fair question, but perhaps his spring training might provide some hints. All signs point to his being worthy of a top-five selection at his position in fantasy leagues regardless.

Rodon got off to a fantastic start in 2024, going 9-2 with a 2.92 ERA and 1.05 WHIP across his first 80 innings (14 starts). He hit some bumps in the road during the summer months, and his season ended on a sour note with three home runs allowed over 3.1 innings in his lone World Series appearance against the Dodgers. Regardless, his 2024 campaign goes down as a considerable success after back, forearm and hamstring injuries cost him half of the previous year and sapped his effectiveness in his first season with the Yankees. His innings totals and performance have been all over the map throughout his career and he's now 32 years old, but recent history bodes rather favorably since Rodon has provided quality numbers across 30-plus starts in two of the past three years. He tentatively lines up as the Yankees' No. 3 starter entering 2025.

Yelich's troublesome back finally forced him under the knife in August, ending his season. Specifically, the procedure was a microdiscectomy, a spinal surgery to remove part or all of a bulging or herniated disc. While Yelich was still not cleared to swing a bat as of mid-December, the team is expecting him to be ready early on in spring training. The outfielder produced at a high level in between IL stints last season, slashing .315/.406/.504 with 11 homers and 21 steals in just 73 games. The back now being surgically repaired offers hope that Yelich could stay on the field and return to something close to his previous levels of production, though it would be unwise to expect him to return an MVP level for the Brewers at 33 years old.

The most anticipated Japanese hurler in seven seasons, Sasaki makes the jump to MLB after four seasons of a 2.02 ERA and a 32.4% strikeout rate overseas, which included a 19-strikeout perfect game in 2022. Though his velocity dipped slightly in 2024, he made 18 starts and had 10 wins, a 2.35 ERA, a 1.04 WHIP and a 28.7% K rate. Sasaki should immediately slot into the Dodgers rotation with prospective top-10 fantasy value in each start he makes. The primary questions surrounding him are health- and workload-related. Can he blow past 100 IP and secure his place as one of fantasy baseball's premier starters? Or will 2025 serve a stepping stone to a future claim of that status over the next couple of years? Either way, Sasaki should be selected in the middle rounds of 2025 drafts. He's a 23-year-old building block in all dynasty and keeper formats.

Suzuki's name has been mentioned in trade rumors, but the Cubs' asking price is high and justifiably so given he has been well above league average at the plate in each of his three seasons in the majors. Suzuki spent time on the injured list again last season and saw his strikeout rate increase, but he kept his batting average over .280 and reached 20 homers for the second straight year. Taking advantage of the bigger bases and new rules limiting pickoff attempts, Suzuki went from six steals in 2023 to 16 last season. The reason the Cubs are willing to listen at all is his defense in the outfield, which was so shaky that the team decided to move him to designated hitter down the stretch. However, Suzuki has said that he does not want to be a full-time DH, which leaves open questions about his future. No matter where he ends up, Suzuki will be in the lineup nearly every day in 2025 since his bat is too good to keep on the bench.

Chapman didn't sign until March 1 last year, but he didn't let the late start affect him as he went on to achieve his best offensive season this decade. The third baseman popped 27 homers and ranked seventh in the National League in runs scored with 98. He added a speed element last season, swiping 15 bags in 17 attempts, which was rather surprising considering he stole 11 bases in his first seven MLB seasons combined. That said, Chapman is no statue and it's reasonable to think he could reach double-digit steals once again in 2025 considering the recent rule changes facilitating the running game and stolen bases in particular. The rest of Chapman's game looks fairly stable, including playing time given his excellent defense at the hot corner. Expect a relatively low average but useful counting stats in his age-32 season.

Who'd have thought that the same Astros pitcher who surrendered nine runs without escaping the first inning of an April 2024 start would go on to score the 10th-most fantasy points among pitchers across the season's final five months? The introduction of a sinker in May played a big part in that, giving Brown a pitch to minimize hard contact to go along with his 96-mph fastball and whiff-generating knuckle curve. With his more balanced repertoire, he's now capable of top-25 fantasy SP numbers on the high end of his valuation curve. Brown is well worth a mid-round selection in all formats.

Turang is a throwback to 1980s baseball in that he makes the most of his speed. He is a pesky hitter who will work counts, fight off pitches and then put one into play, often to the opposite field, before turning on the burners. Turang plays within himself, realizing that double-digit homers are likely out of the picture most seasons, though his profile leaves him very much at the mercy of BABIP fortunes. Turang strikes out approximately once every five at bats, yet only Jake Cronenworth has a lower batting average over the past two seasons for all players with similar strikeout rates or better. The difference with most of the other names on the list is they make more consistent hard contact while Turang's contact metrics are all bottom 20th percentile. This profile fits at the bottom third of the lineup, leaving him plenty of chances to run but also making it difficult to reach even 80 runs scored.

The aging curve appears to have taken hold with Goldschmidt, as his age-37 season saw him post his worst strikeout, walk and home run rates and the lowest isolated power and batting averages of his 14-year MLB career. He did, however, hit 20 home runs across his final 117 games, while mashing lefties (.295/.366/.473), and the move from Busch Stadium to Yankee Stadium should only help him in terms of park factors. Goldschmidt might have one more top-10 fantasy 1B season left in his bat, though his recent trend makes him a wiser player to target for your mixed-league corner infield position.

Ruiz had a bout with the flu early on last season which cost him multiple weeks and caused him to lose nearly 20 pounds. In the end, his OPS fell by nearly 100 points from 2023, though he rebounded a bit in the second half, and it's fair to wonder how much the influenza and subsequent weight loss affected his play. Part of the Nationals' return from the Dodgers in the 2021 Trea Turner-Max Scherzer trade, Ruiz has not quite developed as expected, offensively or defensively. Ruiz makes consistent contact at the plate and packs some power, but a low walk rate drags down his OBP. Signed to a long-term extension in March of 2023, Ruiz will have every chance to rebound and continue his maturation as a player, but at 26 years old, the clock is ticking for him to prove he can make it as a No. 1 catcher.

Many drafters will seen Berrios' name and shrug before moving on to search for a player with more upside. Berrios is an old standby entering his 10th major-league season, but he is coming off an impressive 2024 season in which he won 16 games, tied for second in the American League. He has been consistent with his workload, making exactly 32 starts in each of the last six full MLB seasons, though the same can't quite be said for performance after Berrios led the AL in hits and earned runs allowed in a disastrous first full year with Toronto in 2022. That season shows a very real downside, but Berrios has steadied himself and once again looks like a viable if unexciting pick to help round out a fantasy pitching staff in 2025.

Shaw, the Cubs' first-round pick in the 2023 amateur draft, enters 2025 as a strong candidate to start at third base on Opening Day. After setting Maryland's all-time home run record (53), he managed .357/.400/.618 rates, eight homers and 15 steals across 38 minor league games in his pro debut, then followed it up with a 21-HR, 31-SB 2024 in which he acclimated himself well in 35 season-ending games of Triple-A ball. Shaw's well-rounded skill set appeals to any fantasy format and, while his speed might be his most bankable immediate tool, he could quickly develop in the power department. He's a dynasty building block and a late-round flier, even in ESPN standard redraft leagues.

The ?Pasquatch? is an underrated hitter, especially for points-based scoring. Coming off a 2023 that saw him miss more than three months due to shoulder surgery, Pasquantino joined Yandy Diaz as the only qualified hitters in baseball with at least a 45% hard-hit but no greater than a 15% whiff rate on swings, even if his rotisserie numbers weren't anything special. Unfortunately, further bad luck in the injury department still holds him back as he missed September thanks to a broken thumb. With greater luck in 2025, he has the skills and the prime-age status to become a top-five points based (and top-10 rotisserie) first baseman. Consider taking Pasquantino in the early rounds in points leagues.

The breakthrough didn't appear to happen for Pfaadt during his first full MLB season and, if you consider surface numbers only, his 6.60 ERA across his final 12 starts was unsightly. A check beneath the hood, however, reveals signs of growth that might ultimately lead to a front-of-a-fantasy-rotation role as early as 2025. Thanks to increased sinker usage, he added 10% to his ground-ball rate, and he boosted his strikeout rate during the season's second half, exemplified by his registering three double-digit strikeout performances over his final nine starts. Pfaadt, whom scouts regarded highly at the time of his MLB debut, is one of the better profit-potential starters you'll find in the middle rounds of mixed leagues.

When the curtain closes on Harper's career, he's going to go down as one of the all-time greats, even if during its course it felt like he sometimes fell shy of expectations. Across just the past 10 seasons, Harper has five seasons of 30-plus homers, six of at least a .280 batting average, and five with at least a .900 OPS. The only other player who can make that same claim during that time span is Mike Trout. Now 32, Harper continues to possess elite contact and a patient approach, meaning he should have a few more solid fantasy seasons ahead of him. That he bats in the heart of a still-productive Phillies lineup, in their homer-friendly venue, certainly helps his early-round valuation.

Cease rebounded from a disappointing 2023 with a 2024 that, by many measures, was every bit as meaningful as his breakthrough 2022. Though his ERA (3.47) paled in comparison to 2022 (2.20), he set personal bests with his 8.5% walk rate and 1.07 WHIP. He recaptured the near-entirety of his lost fastball velocity, elevated his ground-ball rate to its highest number since his 2019 debut year, and averaged a near-identical number of innings per start (5.7). Best yet, Cease finished the year on a high note, posting a 2.58 ERA across his final 15 starts. He's also one of the game's most durable starters, having made at least 32 starts in each of the past four years. Cease is a bona fide fantasy staff ace and one well worth a pick in the opening rounds.

Clase is the quintessential example of why fantasy managers shouldn't put too much stock into postseason performance. The regular season's most dominating closer -- his 469 fantasy points were 43 more than the next-closest reliever and his 0.61 ERA was third-best in history among pitchers with at least 50 IP -- he was touched up for two losses, one blown save and a 9.00 ERA across seven October appearances. Chalk that up to a pair of ill-placed sliders and an Aaron Judge wall-scraper, as Clase's 100-mph cutter and slider are otherwise typically next-to-impossible to hit. He's among the best at his craft, and, on a Guardians team sure to be scratching and clawing for W's yet again in 2025, he's as good an investment as closers come.

Be it by design or happenstance, Schwarber's groundball rate last year was his highest in a full season since 2018. Coupled with a career-high hard-hit rate on grounders, Schwarber posted the second-best batting average of his career. His power dipped, but Schwarber's 38 homers were still the eighth most in MLB last season and his quality of contact remained elite. The overall improvement stemmed from hitting southpaws better than right-handers for the first time in his career. Splits like this are often anomalies, so expect regression as Schwarber's platoon splits likely revert to career levels. Keep in mind too that drafting Schwarber means locking up the utility spot since he has lost outfield eligibility entering 2025.

Consistency is tough to find in the late innings. Even the greats like Hader endure some statistical variance -- he had a 5.22 ERA in a difficult 2022 season -- and it comes with the territory of facing the best hitters in the world in the highest-leverage spots night after night. Hader tallied 34 saves in his first year with Houston and has now racked up 30-plus saves in each of the last five full MLB seasons. The left-hander occasionally toes the line with walks and home runs, but his sinking fastball and swing-and-miss slider form a highly effective 1-2 punch. While the Astros have done some retooling this winter, but there is little reason to think Hader won't be the closer for Houston in 2025, with the flexibility and dominance to exceed 100 strikeouts in relief.

A popular pick for AL Rookie of the Year honors entering last season, Caminero's ascent to Tampa Bay was instead delayed by a pair of IL trips due to quadriceps injuries while in Triple-A. He finally got his MLB chance in August, delivering what would have been better-than-70th-percentile Statcast Barrel and hard-hit rates with an above-average contact rate that illustrates his massive offensive upside. Caminero should begin 2025 promised the Rays' everyday 3B role, as well as a heart-of-the-order lineup position. A significant step forward should be well within his reach. He's a potential top-10 positional fantasy option, regardless of format.

Diaz's first season back following right patellar tendon surgery looked shaky on its surface, but his underlying skills nevertheless had the look of a top-shelf closer. A trio of hideous early-season outings bloated his ERA, and a shoulder impingement cost him a few weeks shortly thereafter, but across the season's final three-plus months he had 15 saves (with a 2.41 ERA) and he tied for 11th in RP fantasy points. A winter of rest could do a world of good for Diaz, granting him a full ramping-up process and typical spring training. He'll return as the Mets' closer, a role from which he has twice struck out 90-plus hitters and twice saved 30-plus games (and don't forget he also had one season of each with the Mariners). He should be drafted among the first at his position in fantasy leagues.

Glasnow's season was cut short in August by a right elbow injury, one first labeled as tendonitis but later diagnosed as a sprain following a failed attempt at a return. He said in an offseason interview that imaging in late October appeared to show the elbow being fully healed. While he set a new career high in innings last season before going down, that number being just 134 tells the story. Glasnow had Tommy John surgery in 2021 after missing time earlier in his career with shoulder and forearm trouble, flashing consistent brilliance in between. He had been trending in the right direction with his workload since TJS and proved to be a nice fit in Los Angeles, but his latest injury makes expectations tough to pin down entering 2025. Even if the talented 6-foot-8 righty is healthy and cruising, the Dodgers will probably need to limit him at some point given his injury history.

Once a first-round stalwart, Bichette is coming off a terrible season ravaged by injuries. A .599 OPS after a three-year mark of .815 is especially troublesome, though a 43.5 percent hard-hit rate last season offers hope, as does a clean bill of health after finger surgery. At least doubling last season's 4.4 percent barrel rate is key, and plausible if healthy. Bichette's steals have fallen since he swiped 25 in 26 tries in 2021, but he did notch five bags in what amounts to half a season last year, so a return to double-digit pilfers is in play. By his own account, Bichette tried to be more selective and has vowed to return to a more free-swinging approach. The cost to learn if Bichette re-enters the circle of trust is nominal compared to the reward.

Oh, what his 2024 season might have been had he come to contract terms before March 19. Snell struggled to get up to speed across the season's first three months, spending time on the IL due to adductor and groin issues, but once he found his groove, he managed a 1.23 ERA, a 38.1% strikeout rate and the majors' most fantasy points across his final 14 starts. Snell does have a history of statistical peaks over seasonal portions rather than the whole, but he also possesses multiple Cy Young Awards (2018, 2023), and his second-best-in-baseball 2.82 ERA (minimum 300 innings) across the past three seasons points to him likely being at an overall high point. The Dodgers should do well managing his workload and getting the most out of him, and there's a very real chance that Snell will rebound to rank among his position's best performers.

Miller's campaign was one of the most underappreciated -- not only in 2024, but across all historical rookie RP seasons. He became only the third rookie reliever to manage at least 25 saves, 100 strikeouts and a sub-2.50 ERA (Terry Forster, 1972; Craig Kimbrel, 2011), and among all pitchers with at least 50 IP in 2024, he led in strikeout rate (41.8%), average fastball velocity (100.9 mph) and Statcast-expected ERA (1.77). Miller, who previously had durability concerns, missed only two weeks' time to injury when he fractured his pinky punching a padded table, and a short-relief role seemed to suit his skill set. He has assumed a place as one of the game's best fantasy relievers, and it's a plus for 2025 that his Athletics made winter moves hinting at more of a push to compete.

Few players possess Kwan's elite level of bat control, as evidenced by his 88.9% contact and 28.1% line-drive rates across his three MLB seasons, second- and eighth-best among hitters with at least 900 plate appearances during that time span. At one point in 2024, that put him on a quest for a .400 batting average, before a rise in his launch angle contributed to what was a disappointing, .206 second-half batting average. Kwan's game lacks power, and his raw speed dipped noticeably last season, so he'll need to decide just what kind of hitter he wants to be. As an elite-contact, .300-hitting, 20-SB player with minimal power, he'll remain valuable in any fantasy format, particularly points-based scoring. Consider him in the early rounds in those leagues and slightly later in rotisserie formats.

Contact is the name of the game with Donovan, who sits with a 13.7 percent strikeout rate and an even .280 average through 1,491 career plate appearances. His bat is lacking in terms of thump, however, ranking in the bottom half of the league in average exit velocity and hard-hit rate last season. Donovan logged 652 plate appearances in 2024, second on the team to Paul Goldschmidt, but he managed just 14 homers and five steals, providing fantasy managers with little category juice. He's more than a slap hitter, but Donovan's value is heavily dependent on volume, more so than other hitters in his range. Similar volume is projected in 2025, and eligibility at second base and outfield gives Donovan unique and valuable flexibility.

Flaherty returns to Detroit, where he enjoyed a bounce-back beginning to his 2024, before cooling somewhat after a deadline trade to the Dodgers. Thanks in large part to improved command of his signature slider, his strikeout rate rebounded to near his 2018-19 peak, and he tallied 162 IP, his most in five seasons. Flaherty's 2021-22 injury history might always be a lingering worry, but the improvements he made last season give him good odds of delivering similar numbers this year. He should be selected as a third or fourth fantasy starter in mixed leagues.

Boyd fared remarkably well in his return from June 2023 Tommy John surgery across eight late-season starts and an additional three during the postseason, posting a 2.28 ERA and a 28.2% strikeout rate. Most importantly, both his slider and changeup appeared to have similar life to their pre-surgery models, which was apparently enough for the Cubs to commit $29 million to him across the next two seasons. Boyd's career has reflected much streakiness in terms of his control, and his injury history is a concern. However, so long as he's valued as more of a back-of-your-staff mixed-league type, he's well worth taking a chance.

Friedl was limited to just 85 games last season due to a litany of injuries, beginning with a fractured his wrist in spring training. He also missed time with fractured left thumb and hamstring injury. Since 2022, the lefty-swinging Friedl demonstrated reverse splits, though 82% of his action has been facing right-handers. His Hard Hit and Barrel Rates are among the lowest in MLB, but a 45% flyball level yields power and a 15.2% strikeout rate usually keeps his batting average afloat. Last season's .226 average was deflated with an unlucky .229 BABIP. Friedl's defense is below average, so he needs to hit to play. He's ticketed to hold down the busier side of a right field platoon with Austin Hays, but if Friedl struggles, Hays can cut into Friedl's playing time.

Keller took a significant step forward in 2023, setting career highs across the board, and the Pirates rewarded him with a five-year contract extension prior to last season. He then went onto post similar if slightly disappointing numbers in 2024, as his strikeout rate declined four percentage points and both his ERA and WHIP worsened a bit from the previous season. Keller's average fastball velocity dropped about one mile per hour, and every little bit counts when it comes to velocity. His four-seamer saw the most damage of the fastballs as the league hit 80 points better against that pitch. The right-hander is one of just 13 pitchers to throw at least 175 innings each of the past two seasons and Pittsburgh will be leaning on him to stabilize a young rotation in 2025.

Bogaerts started slowly last season, batting .219/.265/.316 over 47 games, perhaps due to learning a new position after an unexpected shift from shortstop to second base. He then suffered a nasty shoulder injury in May, costing him almost two months. After returning, Bogaerts settled in and hit .299/.338/.432 the rest of the way, in line with his 2023 production. His power never developed as hoped and now it's on the decline with three straight seasons of a falling barrel rate. However, Bogaerts has taken advantage of the rules aiding stolen bases, swiping 32 bases in 37 attempts over the past two years. His bat-to-ball skills are still solid, propping up his floor, but there isn't much upside in power or speed. Dual eligibility adds to Bogaerts' appeal, especially in daily leagues.

Coming off a sizzling finish to 2023 where he scored the most SP fantasy points across his final eight starts, Skubal exploded with a 2024 for the ages, culminating in the AL Cy Young Award. He maintained his 2023 control gains (sixth-ranked 4.6 BB%), added another full tick to his average fastball velocity (third-ranked 96.8 mph), and delivered 20-plus fantasy points in a MLB-leading (tied with Zack Wheeler) 14 of his 31 starts. Best yet, Skubal maintained elite performance across the entire six-month calendar, scoring more points over the Tigers' final 81 regular-season games (279) than in their first 81 (274). It placed him at the forefront of the fantasy SP rankings, though as is true with almost any pitcher these days, he's not completely without risk, with 2017 Tommy John and August 2022 flexor tendon surgeries on his résumé. Hey, sometimes you have to close your eyes tight and roll the dice.

One of the game's most fun, dynamic young talents, De La Cruz burst forth with a historic, breakthrough 2024 that probably didn't even garner the level of attention it deserved. He managed only the seventh season of at least 25 home runs and 60 stolen bases in history, while becoming only the eight different shortstop ever to play at least 160 games at the position while delivering at least 70 extra-base hits. Sure, De La Cruz struck out a ton (an MLB-leading 218 times), as scouts hinted he might, but his excellent raw metrics (contact quality, bat speed, sprint speed) and 23 years of age suggest he has room to grow all-around. It's easy to formulate a first-round case for him in rotisserie leagues, and points-league managers should keep in mind that he finished 47th overall in scoring despite all those K's.

In 2024, many things went just right for Chisholm, a power/speed rotisserie gem for fantasy managers (albeit one with a penchant for injuries). He boosted his contact rate, improving his month-over-month consistency at the plate, played a career-best 147 games, and flourished following a midseason trade to the Yankees, batting .275/.325/.500 with 11 homers and 18 steals in 46 regular-season games in pinstripes. What's more, Chisholm adapted nicely to his new role at third base in New York, and his projected status as their second baseman to begin 2025 might quickly make him eligible at three positions. He might always be at risk of missing time with future ailments, but he's in a great spot for above-average power and elite speed, a combination that gives him top-50 overall upside in rotisserie formats. Bear in mind, however, that Chisholm's value in points-based and sabermetric scoring is a couple of tiers below that.

It has been a whirlwind past two years for Skenes. His LSU Tigers won the 2023 College World Series behind his performance that earned him its Most Outstanding Player Award and he won the Dick Howser Trophy as college baseball's best player. Skenes was then selected No. 1 overall in that July's amateur draft, ultimately reaching the majors with the Pirates just 10 months later. He'd toss six hitless, 11-strikeout frames in only his second start, kicking off a historic campaign that ultimately earned him NL Rookie of the Year honors. Skenes' electric raw stuff (a 99-mph average fastball, slider and splinker) grades among the best in the majors already despite his youth, and he's already drawing favorite's odds for the 2025 Cy Young Award -- a testament to his overwhelming upside. If there's any reason to hesitate in building your fantasy team around him, it's that the Pirates have been cautious with his workload, coupled with the typical worries we have with young pitchers throwing large IP totals. But hey, isn't every pitcher an injury risk to some degree?

Rutschman's smooth, year-over-year ascent to the top of the fantasy catcher rankings hit a roadblock last June. Through his first 77 games, he was batting .300/.351/.480 with 15 home runs and was the top-scoring fantasy catcher. After being struck on the hand with a foul tip, however, he hit just .189/.279/.280 with four homers over his final 71 games. Given the injury, it's rational to forgive Rutschman for the sluggish finish. Even though his spring training bears closer watching than usual, he's a prime-age 27 after being the No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 amateur draft. He has drawn rave reviews from scouts for years, so it's easy to make the case that Rutschman remains a fantasy building block and a sound early-round pick regardless of format.

Bregman's elite plate discipline makes him a valued points-league fantasy player. However, he was only 56th in scoring in 2024, after finishing top-30 in four of the previous six seasons. Maybe his middling contact-quality metrics have begun to catch up with him? A .276/.325/.532, 17-HR performance across his final 62 games offered encouragement that his 2022-24 baselines can be repeated, but the fact remains that he hasn't had a better-than-46th-percentile Statcast Barrel or better-than-51st-percentile hard hit rate since 2018. Where Bregman signs as a free agent will have a say in his fantasy utility -- players with his on-base skills fluctuate more in value based upon who hits behind them and how often their teams' lineups turn over. Until that's known, he's an early-round pick in points leagues and more of a borderline top-100 type in rotisserie.

Arozarena's stock has fallen in the past calendar year. He got off to a brutal start to 2024 with a .461 OPS through the end of April and the Rays later traded him to the Mariners for a pair of prospects and a player to be named later, in line with their usual modus operandi. The outfielder first broke out in the 2020 playoffs when he hit 10 homers, most in postseason history, and in the years since he's turned in four consecutive 20-20 seasons. However, T-Mobile Park in Seattle was the worst in baseball for offense last season by MLB's own park factors, and the lineup around him is underwhelming. Worst of all for his long-term outlook, Arozarena's defense has been dismal in recent years, wiping out a lot of his value to real-world teams. Eventually, that will cost him playing time and the volume will no longer be there to prop him up.

Batting average used to be the ultimate measure of a hitter, but times have changed. Arraez, the three-time reigning batting champion, is now often referred to dismissively as a one-trick pony by fans and fantasy players. That may seem harsh, but there is no getting around the fact that Arraez's batting averages have been empty. Real GMs have found themselves coming to terms with his limitations as a player, with Arraez having already been traded twice and also mentioned in the rumor mill this winter. He added a little bit of speed last season, but Arraez has reached double-digit homers only once, and a low walk rate drags down his OBP. Helping his case is eligibility at both first base and second base entering 2025.

One of baseball's best contact hitters, Hoerner has managed back-to-back top-80 fantasy seasons (in both roto and points-based formats) despite the fact that he hit just 16 home runs combined over those years. No, he's no power source, but his plate approach fuels a consistently solid batting average, his above-average speed and smarts on the bases make him a strong source of steals, and his status in the upper third of the Cubs lineup fuels a good number of plate appearances and runs scored. Hoerner's biggest knock entering 2025 is that he's coming off October flexor tendon surgery, which could threaten his Opening Day status. If he's looking good in March, however, he's one of the game's more underrated players, and well worth an early-round pick.

Signed by the Royals at the end of January, Estevez figures to battle Lucas Erceg, primarily, for saves to begin 2025, and his eight-digit salary probably gives him a leg up in that competition. Estevez managed a career-best 27.8% strikeout rate in his first full season as a closer in 2023, then added enough gains in terms of control last year to serve as a competent, well above-average closer. Fantasy managers will want to monitor the Royals' bullpen pecking order through the Cactus League schedule -- saves carry a three-point advantage over holds in ESPN standard leagues -- but regardless of role, Estevez is a reliever well worth taking in the late rounds.

Strictly in terms of shutting the door and securing wins for his team, Finnegan has been one of the top closers in baseball over the past couple years. In fact, only Emmanuel Clase, Josh Hader and Raisel Iglesias have more saves than Finnegan since the start of the 2023 season. However, he lacks the swing-and-miss dominance typically associated with the late innings. The Nationals declined to tender Finnegan a contract for 2025 despite his success, making him a free agent in November. Finnegan reined in the long ball and did not allow a single homer over the final two months of last season, but it seems more likely than not that he's without a closer job to begin 2025 since the underlying numbers are not closer-worthy. His experience and success in the ninth should keep him on your radar, but at best he's a speculative endgame pick until there's clarity on his situation.

Gurriel had another productive if unspectacular season at the plate for the Diamondbacks in 2024. He contributes to all five categories, but his batting average is arguably his best contribution to a fantasy team's bottom line. Gurriel has been one of the better contact hitters in baseball in recent seasons, but his aversion to walks limits his ability to reach base. His walk and chase rates were both in the bottom 25th percentile last season and do not show any signs of improvement in the near future. The outfielder is at his best when he is facing southpaws, as he has hit .317/.366/.485 against them over the past two seasons compared to .250/.294/.434 against righties.  The retooled lineup in Arizona could have Gurriel hitting cleanup this season which would allow him to potentially drive in 85 runs for the first time in his career. However, some of the leading indicators around his quality of contact trended in a concerning direction in 2024.

The top catcher in all of fantasy baseball not long ago, Realmuto has fallen back to the pack entering 2025. He underwent surgery on his right knee in June and missed five weeks, which kept him under 100 games played last season. The big problem, presumably related to the knee, is that he went from 16 steals in 2023 to a mere two last year. He can still hit for impressive pop, but speed from the catcher position was such a big part of his appeal previously, and while that aspect of his game may not be completely gone, it figures to be diminished in his mid-30s. Further, his walk rate has dipped in recent years, taking his on-base percentage along with it, and Realmuto has slid down the Phillies' order as a result.

Many were expecting another step forward for Hayes in 2024 after his strong 2023 campaign in which he set career highs in everything but steals. However, a bothersome back had other plans for Hayes and he eventually succumbed to those issues in mid-August. Hitters absolutely need a healthy core and back in order to drive the baseball. If anything, the fact Hayes had nearly league-average exit velocity despite the back troubles speaks to his natural talent. Hayes could absolutely repeat his 2023 numbers if his back troubles are behind him and he can resume his regular spot in the daily lineup. His overall profile still fits better down in the lineup than it does toward the top, but one should not be judged on the merits of a season riddled with back troubles when we have seen recent success from the same player.
